title: Organ systems: how the organs inside you share parts and work together

summary.text: Sitting still, you can count aloud for about 20 seconds on one breath. Straight after step-ups, you manage far fewer. Your lungs have not shrunk, so why? In this unit you will time your own voice before and after exercise, share out 100 beans as blood, and sort organs into the systems they work in.
summary.art: A girl sitting on a step with a hand on her chest, counting aloud, while her mother holds a phone stopwatch. A faint outline inside the girl shows her lungs, windpipe and voice box.

intro.hook: Say 'aaaa' in one long, steady sound. In the middle of it, swallow. Your voice stops, every time. Why can you not make a sound and swallow at the same moment?
intro.text: Your throat is one passage with two jobs. Air passes through it to the lungs, and food passes through it to the stomach. Your voice box sits at the top of the windpipe, so your voice needs the same air as your breathing. In this unit you learn the organ systems of the body and the organs in each one. You also find the places where two systems share one part. You time how long you can count on one breath, at rest and after exercise. You share out 100 beans to see where the blood goes when you run.
intro.art: A child with two fingers resting on the front of her throat, mouth open in a long 'aaaa', with a small arrow showing the bump in her throat moving up.

outcomes: I can name the main organ systems, the main organs in each, and each system's job.
I can trace food, air, blood and urine through the right organs, including the heart's four chambers.
I can name the three main parts of the brain, and tell voluntary muscles from involuntary muscles.
I can name the reproductive organs correctly and say how a baby begins.
I can give examples of an organ that works in two systems, such as the throat and the pancreas.
I can explain, using my One Breath Count, why I cannot talk for long straight after exercise.
I can explain how the systems hand things to each other, and how the blood is shared out.
I can run a fair test on my own body, average my tries, and explain what I found.

terms.meaning: A body part that does a special job. An organ is built from several kinds of tissue.
terms.example: The heart, the liver, a kidney, the skin and an eye are all organs.
terms.art: A heart, a liver, a kidney and an eye drawn side by side, each with a small label.

terms.meaning: A group of cells of the same kind that work together. Organs are made of tissues.
terms.example: Muscle tissue can shorten. Nerve tissue carries signals. The heart contains both.
terms.art: A zoom-in circle on a heart wall showing long striped muscle cells lying side by side.

terms.meaning: A group of organs that work together on one big job for the whole body.
terms.example: The mouth, food pipe, stomach, intestines, liver and pancreas make up the digestive system.
terms.art: A body outline with the digestive organs coloured in one colour and joined by a line.

terms.meaning: A place where two bones meet. A movable joint lets the bones move. A fixed joint does not.
terms.example: Your knee and elbow are movable joints. The joints between the bones of your skull are fixed.
terms.art: A bent knee joint beside the zigzag lines where skull bones meet.

terms.meaning: A muscle that you move when you choose to. Voluntary muscles are joined to bones.
terms.example: The biceps in your upper arm is a voluntary muscle. You decide when to lift a tumbler.
terms.art: An arm lifting a steel tumbler, with the upper arm muscle shaded.

terms.meaning: A muscle that works without your choosing. It keeps working while you sleep.
terms.example: The muscles in the walls of your stomach and intestines are involuntary. So is the muscle of your heart.
terms.art: A sleeping child with her heart and stomach shown faintly, small movement lines around both.

terms.meaning: The tube that carries air from the throat down to the lungs. Doctors call it the trachea.
terms.example: You can feel the hard rings of your windpipe at the front of your neck, just above your chest.
terms.art: A neck seen from the front with the ringed windpipe drawn inside, dividing into two tubes at the bottom.

terms.meaning: Tiny air bags at the ends of the air tubes in the lungs. Oxygen passes from them into the blood.
terms.example: A grown-up's lungs hold hundreds of millions of alveoli. One alone is called an alveolus.
terms.art: A bunch of tiny round air bags like grapes, wrapped in a net of fine red and blue blood vessels.

terms.meaning: The chambers of the heart. The two atria at the top receive blood. The two ventricles below pump it out.
terms.example: The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, so its wall is the thickest.
terms.art: A heart cut open to show four rooms, the two upper ones small and the two lower ones larger.

terms.meaning: Three kinds of blood vessel. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins carry it back. Capillaries are the finest vessels, and they join the arteries to the veins.
terms.example: The pulse in your wrist is an artery. The blue lines on the back of your hand are veins.
terms.art: A thick red tube branching into a net of hair-thin vessels and joining again into a blue tube.

terms.meaning: One of two bean-shaped organs at the back, just under the ribs. Kidneys filter the blood and make urine.
terms.example: Each of your kidneys is about the size of your own fist.
terms.art: A child's back with two bean shapes drawn just under the lowest ribs, one on each side of the backbone.

terms.meaning: A waste that the liver makes when the body breaks down protein. The kidneys remove urea from the blood.
terms.example: Urea leaves the body dissolved in urine.
terms.art: A liver passing small dots into a blood vessel, and a kidney passing the same dots into a tube leading down.

terms.meaning: The largest part of the brain, at the top. The cerebrum does thinking, remembering, speaking, sensing and chosen movement.
terms.example: When you work out 100 take away 3, your cerebrum is working.
terms.art: A side view of a brain with the large wrinkled top part coloured.

terms.meaning: A smaller part of the brain, at the back and below the cerebrum. The cerebellum keeps movement smooth and keeps your balance.
terms.example: When you ride a bicycle without thinking about each push, your cerebellum is helping.
terms.art: A side view of a brain with the small rounded part at the lower back coloured.

terms.meaning: The stalk at the base of the brain that joins it to the spinal cord. The brainstem runs breathing, heartbeat and swallowing.
terms.example: Your brainstem keeps you breathing all night while you sleep.
terms.art: A side view of a brain with the stalk at the bottom coloured, leading down into the spinal cord.

terms.meaning: A chemical message made by a gland and carried in the blood. A hormone changes what another organ does.
terms.example: Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas. Insulin tells cells to take sugar out of the blood.
terms.art: A small gland releasing dots into a blood vessel, and the dots arriving at a muscle far away.

terms.meaning: The passage behind the nose and mouth. Air and food both pass through the throat. Doctors call it the pharynx.
terms.example: The air you breathe and the idli you swallow both cross your throat.
terms.art: A side view of a head showing one passage behind the mouth that splits lower down into a front tube and a back tube.

terms.meaning: The top of the windpipe, where two folds called the vocal cords sit. Air passing out makes the folds shake, and that makes your voice. Doctors call it the larynx.
terms.example: Put your fingers on the front of your throat and hum. The buzzing you feel comes from your voice box.
terms.art: A neck with a small box drawn at the top of the windpipe and two folds inside, with air arrows passing up between them.

terms.meaning: A flap behind the tongue. When you swallow, the epiglottis folds down over the opening of the windpipe.
terms.example: The epiglottis is why a mouthful of rasam goes to your stomach and not into your lungs.
terms.art: A side view of a throat during a swallow, with a leaf-shaped flap tipped down over the windpipe and food sliding past behind it.

terms.meaning: The soft tissue inside many bones. Red bone marrow makes new blood cells.
terms.example: The marrow in your hip bones, ribs and backbone makes millions of red blood cells every second.
terms.art: A long bone cut open to show soft red tissue inside, with tiny red discs leaving into a blood vessel.

terms.meaning: The form in which the liver and the muscles store sugar. The liver turns glycogen back into sugar when the blood needs more.
terms.example: Between dinner and breakfast, your liver keeps your blood sugar steady from its glycogen.
terms.art: A liver holding small bundles like bunches of beads, with single beads leaving into a blood vessel.

terms.meaning: The organs that make it possible to have a baby. In a male they are the testes and the penis. In a female they are the ovaries, the fallopian tubes, the uterus and the vagina.
terms.example: An ovary releases an egg. A testis makes sperm.
terms.art: Two plain outline diagrams, one of the female reproductive organs and one of the male, each with label lines.

explanations.concept: Cells, tissues, organs and organ systems
explanations.definition: An organ system is a group of organs that work together on one big job for the whole body.
explanations.description: Your body is built in levels. The smallest living unit is the cell, and a grown-up has about 30 trillion of them. Cells of one kind form a tissue, such as muscle tissue or nerve tissue. Several tissues together form an organ, such as the heart. Several organs together form an organ system. Books usually list about ten systems. This unit uses nine: skeletal, muscular, digestive, respiratory, circulatory, excretory, nervous, hormone and reproductive. Doctors call the hormone system the endocrine system. The skin, hair and nails are often counted as one more system. No organ system can keep the body alive without the others.
examples: Level 1 is a cell. One example is a single heart muscle cell.
Level 2 is a tissue. One example is heart muscle tissue.
Level 3 is an organ. One example is the heart.
Level 4 is an organ system. The heart, the blood vessels and the blood together form the circulatory system.
explanations.art: Four drawings in a row joined by arrows: one muscle cell, a patch of muscle tissue, a heart, and a body outline with the heart and blood vessels.

explanations.concept: The skeletal and muscular systems: frame and movement
explanations.definition: The skeletal system is the bones and joints. The muscular system is the muscles that move the bones and the muscles inside organs.
explanations.description: A grown-up has 206 bones. A newborn baby has about 300 separate pieces, and many of them join as the child grows. The skeleton does five jobs. It gives the body its shape. It protects soft organs: the skull guards the brain, and the ribs guard the heart and lungs. It gives the muscles something to pull on. Its marrow makes blood cells. It also stores calcium. Bones meet at joints. The knee and the elbow bend like a door hinge. The shoulder and the hip turn in a circle. The joints of the skull are fixed and do not move. Strong bands called ligaments tie bone to bone, and cords called tendons tie muscle to bone. A muscle can only pull, never push. So muscles work in pairs. The biceps bends the elbow, and the triceps at the back straightens it. Muscles joined to bones are voluntary: you choose when to move them. The muscles in the walls of the stomach, the intestines and the blood vessels are involuntary. Heart muscle is a third kind. Heart muscle is involuntary and never rests.
examples: Voluntary muscles include the muscles of your arms, legs, fingers, tongue and face.
Involuntary muscles include the ones that squeeze food along your intestines.
Some muscles can work both ways. You can blink on purpose, but your eyelids also blink without you choosing.
A fixed joint is one that does not move. The wavy lines where the bones of your skull meet are fixed joints.
explanations.art: A child bending her elbow to lift a bag, with the bones of the arm drawn inside and the front muscle shown short and fat, the back muscle long and thin.

explanations.concept: The digestive system: from food to blood
explanations.definition: The digestive system breaks food into pieces small enough to pass into the blood, and pushes out what is left.
explanations.description: Food travels along one tube. The tube runs from the mouth down the food pipe to the stomach. It goes on through the small intestine and the large intestine, and ends at the anus. Teeth break the food, and saliva wets it and starts to digest starch. The stomach churns the food with acid. In the small intestine, which is several metres long in a grown-up, juices finish the digesting. The digested food passes through the wall into the blood. The large intestine takes back water. What is left leaves as faeces. Two organs help without food ever passing through them. The liver makes bile, which breaks fat into tiny droplets. The pancreas makes a juice that digests starch, protein and fat. The liver is the heaviest organ inside the body. A grown-up's liver weighs about one and a half kilograms. It also stores sugar as glycogen, and it changes many poisons into safer substances.
examples: Rice is starch. Digestion cuts starch into sugar, and the sugar enters the blood.
Dal and egg hold protein. Digestion cuts protein into small units called amino acids.
The skin of a sweetcorn kernel is not digested. It leaves the body as it came in.
explanations.art: A body outline with one continuous tube from mouth to bottom, the liver and pancreas drawn beside it with small arrows sending juices into the tube.

explanations.concept: The respiratory system: air in, air out
explanations.definition: The respiratory system brings oxygen from the air into the blood. It also takes carbon dioxide out of the blood.
explanations.description: Air enters through the nose, where hairs and sticky mucus catch dust. The air passes through the throat and the voice box, and down the windpipe. The windpipe splits into two tubes called bronchi, one for each lung. The tubes branch again and again and end in tiny air bags called alveoli. Each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries. Oxygen passes from the air in the alveolus into the blood. Carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the air. This swap is called gas exchange. The lungs have no muscle of their own. A sheet of muscle under them, the diaphragm, pulls down, and the rib muscles lift the ribs. The chest gets bigger and air flows in. When these muscles relax, air flows out. The brainstem sets the pace. It measures carbon dioxide in the blood, and when there is more, it makes you breathe faster and deeper.
examples: The path of air: nose, throat, voice box, windpipe, bronchi, alveoli.
Out of every 100 parts of the air you breathe in, about 21 are oxygen. In the air you breathe out, about 16 are oxygen.
The urge to breathe after a run comes mainly from extra carbon dioxide in the blood.
explanations.art: A chest with the windpipe dividing into two branching trees inside the lungs, and one zoom-in circle showing a tiny air bag wrapped in fine blood vessels.

explanations.concept: The circulatory system: one pump, two loops
explanations.definition: The circulatory system is the heart, the blood vessels and the blood. It carries oxygen, food, wastes, heat and hormones between all the organs.
explanations.description: The heart is a muscle with four chambers. The right side and the left side are two pumps joined together. Blood from the body, low in oxygen, enters the right atrium. It passes down to the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs. In the lungs the blood picks up oxygen. It returns to the left atrium and passes down to the left ventricle. The left ventricle pumps it out to the whole body. So blood passes through the heart twice on each trip: once on the way to the lungs, and once on the way to the body. Valves in the heart open one way only, so blood cannot flow back. Arteries carry blood away from the heart. They branch into capillaries, vessels so fine that red blood cells pass in single file. Through the thin capillary walls, the blood gives oxygen and food to the cells and takes their wastes. Veins carry the blood back. A child of ten has about 2 litres of blood, and a grown-up about 5 litres.
examples: The loop to the lungs: right ventricle, lungs, left atrium.
The loop to the body: left ventricle, body, right atrium.
The 'lub-dub' a doctor hears is the sound of heart valves closing.
explanations.art: A simple diagram of a four-chambered heart with a small loop going up to the lungs and a large loop going down to the body, low-oxygen blood in blue and oxygen-rich blood in red.

explanations.concept: The excretory system: taking wastes out of the blood
explanations.definition: The excretory system removes the wastes that cells make. It also keeps the right amount of water and salt in the body.
explanations.description: Cells make wastes as they work. When the body breaks down protein, the liver turns the leftover part into urea. Blood carries the urea to the two kidneys. Each kidney holds about a million tiny filters. The filters let water, salt, sugar and urea out of the blood. Then the kidney takes back almost all the water and everything else the body needs. What is left is urine. Urine runs down two tubes called ureters into the bladder, a bag of muscle that stores it. Urine leaves through a tube called the urethra. A grown-up's kidneys filter about 180 litres of liquid a day. From this they make about one and a half litres of urine. Other organs remove wastes too. The lungs breathe out carbon dioxide. The skin loses water and salt as sweat. Faeces are different. Most of what is in faeces was never inside the body's cells. So scientists do not call it excretion.
examples: The path of urine: kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra.
On a hot day you sweat more, so your kidneys make less urine, and it is darker.
A person can live well with one healthy kidney.
explanations.art: A body outline seen from the back with two kidneys, two thin tubes leading down to a bladder, and a short tube leaving it.

explanations.concept: The nervous system and the hormone system: two ways to send messages
explanations.definition: The nervous system sends fast signals along nerves. The hormone system sends slower chemical messages through the blood.
explanations.description: The nervous system is the brain, the spinal cord and the nerves. The brain has three main parts. The cerebrum is the large wrinkled part at the top. It thinks, remembers, speaks, makes sense of what the eyes and ears send, and starts movements you choose. The cerebellum sits at the back, under the cerebrum. It keeps your balance and makes practised movements smooth. The brainstem joins the brain to the spinal cord. It runs breathing, heartbeat and swallowing, and you do not have to think about any of them. The spinal cord runs down inside the backbone. Nerves branch from it to every part of the body. The hormone system is a set of glands. A gland makes a hormone and releases it into the blood. The hormone travels everywhere, but only organs with the right receptors answer. A nerve signal arrives in a fraction of a second. A hormone takes seconds, minutes or hours, and its effect lasts longer.
examples: Your cerebrum is working when you read this sentence and decide to turn the page.
Your cerebellum is working when you catch a ball, or walk without watching your feet.
Your brainstem is working when you breathe while you sleep.
Adrenaline is a hormone made by the adrenal glands. It makes your heart beat faster when you get a fright.
explanations.art: A side view of a head showing the brain in three colours, top, lower back and stalk, with the spinal cord running down and small glands marked in the neck and above the kidneys.

explanations.concept: The reproductive system: how a new person begins
explanations.definition: The reproductive system is the set of organs that makes it possible to have a baby.
explanations.description: This is the one system that differs between male and female bodies. In a female body, two ovaries hold tiny eggs. Each ovary is joined to the uterus by a fallopian tube. The uterus, also called the womb, is a bag of muscle where a baby grows. The vagina is the passage that leads from the uterus to the outside. In a male body, two testes make sperm. The sperm leave the body through the penis. A baby begins when one sperm from the father joins one egg from the mother. The joined cell divides again and again and settles in the wall of the uterus. There the baby grows for about nine months. These organs are present from birth, but they start their full work only in the teenage years. Hormones from the brain, the ovaries and the testes start that change. For the parent: use the correct names calmly, as you would say 'elbow' or 'kidney'. Children who know the right words can ask clear questions and can tell a trusted adult if something is wrong.
examples: Female organs: ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, vagina.
Male organs: testes, penis.
The ovaries and the testes also make hormones, so they belong to the hormone system as well.
explanations.art: Two plain, labelled outline diagrams side by side: the female organs with ovaries, tubes, uterus and vagina, and the male organs with testes and penis.

explanations.concept: One organ, two systems: parts that are shared
explanations.definition: Many organs do work for more than one organ system.
explanations.description: The lists of systems look tidy in a book, but several organs appear on two lists. The throat carries air for the respiratory system and food for the digestive system. When you swallow, the voice box lifts, the epiglottis folds over the windpipe, and breathing stops for about one second. The voice box makes your voice from breathed-out air, so talking and breathing share one stream of air. The pancreas makes digestive juice, and it also makes the hormones insulin and glucagon. Bones belong to the skeleton, and their marrow makes the cells of the blood. The diaphragm is a muscle, and it does the work of breathing. The liver makes bile for digestion, makes urea for the kidneys to remove, and stores sugar for every organ. The kidneys make urine. They also make a hormone that tells the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. When two systems share one part, they cannot both use it fully at the same moment. In the One Breath Count you measure this. After exercise, your body needs fresh air for gas exchange, so less of each breath is left for your voice.
examples: The throat works for the digestive system and for the respiratory system.
The pancreas works for the digestive system and for the hormone system.
The thigh bone works for the skeletal system and for the circulatory system, because the marrow inside it makes blood cells.
The ovaries and the testes work for the reproductive system and for the hormone system.
explanations.art: A body outline with five organs circled, throat, pancreas, thigh bone, diaphragm and kidney, each circle drawn half in one colour and half in another.

explanations.concept: Systems working together: handing things over
explanations.definition: Every job the body does needs several organ systems, each passing something to the next.
explanations.description: Take climbing three floors of stairs. The cerebrum decides to climb, and nerves carry signals to the leg muscles. The muscles pull on the bones. Working muscle cells need more oxygen and more sugar. The lungs pass oxygen to the blood. The small intestine passed sugar to the blood after breakfast, and the liver adds more from its glycogen. The heart pumps the blood to the muscles. The muscles hand back carbon dioxide and heat. The blood carries the carbon dioxide to the lungs and the heat to the skin. The brainstem senses the extra carbon dioxide and speeds up the breathing and the heart. The blood is also shared out in a new way, compared with when the body is resting. At rest, a grown-up's heart pumps about 5 litres a minute. The gut, the liver and the kidneys take almost half of it. In hard exercise the heart can pump about 20 litres a minute, and roughly four fifths goes to the muscles. The gut and the kidneys get less than half of what they had at rest, so digestion slows. The brain gets about the same amount as before. You model this with beans in the Hundred Beans.
examples: When you eat a dosa, your muscles chew it and the digestive system digests it. The blood carries the sugar, and the pancreas sends insulin.
On a hot afternoon, your skin sweats, your kidneys save water, and your brain makes you feel thirsty.
When you get a fright, the adrenal glands send adrenaline, your heart speeds up, and your muscles get ready to move.
explanations.art: A girl climbing stairs with small labelled arrows inside her outline: oxygen from lungs to blood, sugar from liver to blood, blood to leg muscles, carbon dioxide back to lungs, heat to skin.

explanations.concept: Organs send each other chemical messages
explanations.description: For a long time, people pictured the brain as the one organ that gives orders. We now know that many organs send messages of their own through the blood. In 1981 Adolfo de Bold and his team in Canada found that the heart makes a hormone. When too much blood stretches the heart, this hormone tells the kidneys to let out more salt and water. In 1994 Jeffrey Friedman's team in New York found leptin. Leptin is a hormone made by body fat that tells the brain how much fat is stored. The stomach and the intestines make hormones that tell the brain about hunger and fullness. Working muscles release chemicals too. Scientists are still finding out what those do. In 2007 Gerard Karsenty's team reported that bone makes a hormone that changes how mice handle sugar. Other teams have not found the same effect, so this one is still argued.
examples: This is settled: the heart, body fat, the gut and the kidneys all make hormones.
This is still argued: whether a hormone from bone changes how the body handles sugar.
This is not yet known: how many such messages there are, and what they all do.

perspectives.explanation: Almost every organ releases chemical messages. The body is run by many organs signalling each other, and the brain is one of them.
Finding a chemical in the blood does not show that it carries a message. Each one must be tested, and some early claims have not held up.

explanations.art: A body outline with thin dotted arrows running between heart and kidneys, fat and brain, stomach and brain, and bone and pancreas, each arrow a different colour.

explanations.description: Many websites say the human body has 78 organs. No group of scientists has agreed on that list. The answer depends on what counts as one organ. Are the 206 bones one organ each, or parts of one skeleton? Is each tooth an organ? In 2016 the Irish surgeon J. Calvin Coffey argued that the mesentery should be counted as an organ. The mesentery is the sheet that holds the intestines in place. Earlier books had described it as several separate pieces. He showed that it is one continuous sheet. In 2018 a team in New York described fluid-filled spaces in the wrappings of organs. They called these spaces a new organ, the interstitium. Many anatomists replied that these spaces were already known and are a tissue, not an organ.
examples: Counted as an organ by everyone: heart, liver, kidney, lung, brain, skin.
Argued: the mesentery, the interstitium, each bone, each tooth.

perspectives.who: Anatomists who want a fixed list
perspectives.explanation: An organ is a body part with its own shape, its own tissues and its own job. With that rule we can count organs, even if the number is argued at the edges.
The body does not come divided into pieces. 'Organ' is a useful word that people apply in different ways, so there is no one true number.

explanations.art: A page of a notebook with a list of organs, some ticked firmly and some marked with a question mark.

explanations.concept: Other animals arrange the same jobs differently
explanations.definition: Every animal must take in food and oxygen, move them around and remove wastes. Different animals use different organs and plans to do it.
explanations.description: Humans are one kind of animal, and our plan is one among many. In whales and dolphins, the windpipe leads to the blowhole on top of the head. Their air and their food take separate paths, so they do not share a throat the way we do. A fish has a heart with two chambers, and the blood makes one loop: heart, gills, body, heart. A frog's heart has three chambers. Birds and mammals have four chambers and two loops. An insect has no lungs. Fine air tubes run from holes along the insect's sides to every part of the body. The insect's blood carries food but almost no oxygen, so breathing and blood are separate there. A bird's lungs are joined to air bags, and air flows through the lungs in one direction. An earthworm breathes through their damp skin, so the skin is their breathing organ.
examples: In a whale, air and food take separate paths.
An insect has air tubes that bring oxygen to the body without using blood.
A fish has a heart with two chambers, and the blood makes one loop.
An earthworm breathes through their skin, so the skin does the work of lungs.
explanations.art: Four small panels: a dolphin with an arrow to the blowhole, a fish with a one-loop blood path, a grasshopper with dots along the side, and an earthworm on damp soil.

agreed.text: The body is built in levels: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form organ systems.
agreed.evidence: Microscopes show the cells and tissues of every organ. Anatomists have traced how the organs connect for more than 400 years.

agreed.text: Blood passes through the heart twice on each trip: once towards the lungs and once towards the body.
agreed.evidence: William Harvey showed in 1628 that blood goes round in a circle. Today doctors watch the two loops with ultrasound scans.

agreed.text: The throat is shared by air and food, and breathing stops for about a second during every swallow.
agreed.evidence: X-ray films of people swallowing show the voice box lifting and the epiglottis folding over the windpipe. Breathing sensors record the pause.

agreed.text: In hard exercise, the body sends most of the blood to the muscles. The gut and the kidneys get less.
agreed.evidence: Blood flow to each organ has been measured in people at rest and in exercise since the 1940s.

agreed.text: The liver makes sugar and releases it into the blood, as well as making bile.
agreed.evidence: Claude Bernard found sugar in the blood leaving the livers of dogs fed only meat, in 1848. He separated glycogen from liver in 1857.

agreed.text: Organs other than glands also make hormones.
agreed.evidence: The heart's hormone was found in 1981 and the hormone leptin from body fat in 1994. Doctors now measure both in blood tests.

challenging.who: A common belief, and the view of most scientists before the 1850s
challenging.for: It is the simplest picture, and each organ does have a best-known job: the heart pumps, the lungs breathe, the liver makes bile.
challenging.against: Claude Bernard showed that the liver also makes sugar. Since then, more jobs have been found for the pancreas, the kidneys, the bones and the heart.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that every organ does just one thing.

challenging.claim: The human body has exactly 78 organs.
challenging.for: A fixed number is easy to remember, and lists with 78 names do exist.
challenging.against: No scientific body has agreed on a list. In 2016 a surgeon argued that the mesentery is one more organ. The count depends on how you define an organ.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the organs of the body can be counted.

challenging.claim: The brain gives the orders and the other organs only obey.
challenging.who: A common picture of the body
challenging.for: The brain does control breathing, movement and many glands, and damage to the brainstem stops the body working.
challenging.against: The heart, the gut, the fat and the kidneys send hormones that change what the brain does. A heart keeps its own beat, and the gut has hundreds of millions of nerve cells of its own.
challenging.context: This card is about who is in charge inside the body.

challenging.claim: Bone sends a hormone that changes how the body handles sugar.
challenging.who: Gerard Karsenty and his team at Columbia University, from 2007
challenging.for: In their mice, removing the bone protein osteocalcin changed blood sugar and body fat.
challenging.against: In 2020 two other teams made mice without osteocalcin and found normal blood sugar. Nobody has shown the effect clearly in people.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the skeleton also works as a gland.

challenging.claim: The interstitium is a newly found organ.
challenging.who: Neil Theise and a team in New York, in 2018
challenging.for: With a new kind of microscope, they saw fluid-filled spaces inside the living wrappings of organs. Older methods had squashed these spaces flat.
challenging.against: Many anatomists say the fluid between cells was already well known. They add that a set of spaces is a tissue and cannot be called an organ.
challenging.context: This card is about a claim that scientists had missed a whole organ.

big_questions.q: Your throat belongs to the breathing system and to the digestive system. So where does one system end and the next begin?
big_questions.hint: Think about who drew the lists of systems, and why.

big_questions.q: If a surgeon gives you another person's kidney, and it works in you for 20 years, whose kidney is it?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the kidney does all day, and for whom.

big_questions.q: Your heart, lungs and liver work without asking you. Are they doing it, or are you doing it?
big_questions.hint: Try saying 'I digest my food' and then 'my stomach digests my food'. Which sounds more true?

big_questions.q: A whale has separate paths for air and food, and we share one. Is our shared throat a mistake, or does it give us something?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you do with breathed-out air that a path to a blowhole could not do so easily.

big_questions.q: Every organ needs all the others. So is any one organ the most important?
big_questions.hint: Try taking each one away in your mind and see what happens to the rest.

big_questions.q: A city has water pipes, roads, drains and phone lines. In what ways is a city like a body, and in what ways is it not?
big_questions.hint: Think about who planned the city, and whether anyone planned the body.

story.title: Sadugudu on One Breath
story.note: The people in this story are made up. The rule is real. Many people in Tamil Nadu call kabaddi sadugudu. A raider must chant the word aloud on one breath for the whole raid. If the chant stops, the raider is out. In today's professional matches a raid is also limited to 30 seconds by a clock. The science is real too: the voice uses breathed-out air, and after hard running after hard running the body needs fresh air much sooner, so the chant is cut short.
text: In Yazhini's village near Thanjavur, the game was called sadugudu. The school called it kabaddi. Under both names, the rule that mattered was the same.

A raider crosses the middle line alone. She must touch one of the seven girls on the other side and get home again. From the moment she crosses the line until she is back, she must chant the word aloud: sadugudu, sadugudu, sadugudu. She must do it all on a single breath. If the chant stops, or if she takes a second breath, she is out.

Yazhini was ten, and she was the fastest runner in Class 5. She could beat everyone in her lane to the tea shop and back. So when Selvi Akka, who had played for the district, started a girls' team behind the ration shop, Yazhini expected to be its best raider.
She was out in four seconds.
"Sadugudu-sadugudu-sadu..." Then came a gasp, loud enough for both teams to hear. Selvi Akka blew her whistle. Out.

It happened again the next evening, and the evening after that. Yazhini warmed up the way runners do. She sprinted up and down the side of the court until her legs felt quick and light. Then she charged across the line. Her legs were ready every time. Her chant died almost at once.
"My lungs are too small," she told her grandmother that night.
"Then stretch them," said Paati, who believed that most things could be stretched.
So Yazhini practised. She sat under the wall clock and held her breath while the seconds hand went round. Forty seconds. Fifty. By the end of the week she could hold her breath for a full minute.
On the court she still lasted four seconds. It made no sense. A minute at home, and four seconds behind the ration shop.

The best raider on the team turned out to be Kaviya. Kaviya was small, and she came last in every race. Yet Kaviya raided for twenty seconds at a time. Her chant ran on as evenly as a sewing machine. She touched an ankle, turned, and was home before anyone caught her.
On Thursday, Yazhini stubbed her toe on the water pot, and Selvi Akka made her sit out. She sat on the low wall with her foot up and watched Kaviya properly for the first time.

Before each raid, Kaviya stood quite still at the back of the court. She breathed in and out slowly, four or five times. Then she took one more breath, a deep one, and walked to the line. She walked. Kaviya did not run one step until she had to.

Yazhini had been sitting on the wall for ten minutes. Without quite meaning to, she took a breath and began under her voice. Sadugudu, sadugudu, sadugudu. She counted on her fingers. She reached forty-one before she needed air.
Forty-one. On the court she had never passed nine.

She had the same lungs on the wall as on the court. So what was different? On the wall, her legs were doing nothing. On the court, she had always sprinted first. And after a sprint she panted. Everybody did. Straight after a sprint she could not even answer Selvi Akka properly. Her words came out in pieces: "Yes... Akka... I will."

Panting was her body pulling air in and pushing it out, fast, because her legs had used so much. The chant needed the air to go out slowly, a little at a time. The legs and the chant wanted the same breath. And her legs had been spending it before she even reached the line.
On Saturday the girls from Thiruvaiyaru came for the Pongal match. With the score level, Selvi Akka pointed at Yazhini.

Yazhini did not sprint. She stood at the back of the court. "Come on, runner!" a girl on the other side called. Yazhini breathed in and out slowly, five times, until her chest was quiet. She took one deep breath and walked to the line.

"Sadugudu, sadugudu, sadugudu." She kept it soft. She had worked out that a shout spends air faster than a murmur. She took small steps. She let the seven girls shuffle and crouch and wait for the famous charge that did not come.

Somewhere past the fifteenth sadugudu she felt it. It was the first tightness, her chest beginning to ask for air. She knew now what was asking, and she knew it would win in the end. So she did not argue with it. She used her fast legs for one second only. One lunge, one touch on the corner girl's shoulder, three strides, and she was over the line.
"...gudu." And then air, a great deal of it.
The whistle blew. A point.
Kaviya thumped her on the back. "You walked!"
"I ran," said Yazhini, between breaths. "At the end. When I could pay for it."
Selvi Akka only said, "Now you know what the chant is for."
Yazhini thought she did. Whoever made the rule, long ago, had not needed a stopwatch. Every raider carries her own clock in her chest, and running makes it tick faster.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Yazhini thinks her problem is the size of her lungs. Holding her breath for a minute at home does not help. Something else sets the limit on the court. The voice is made by air leaving the lungs through the voice box. So a chant can last only as long as one breath out. After a sprint, the muscles have used oxygen and made carbon dioxide. The brainstem then forces the next breath within seconds. Breathing and speaking share one stream of air, and when the body needs gas exchange urgently, the voice loses. Yazhini wins by starting her raid with quiet breathing, chanting softly and saving her running for the last second.
ask: Why could Yazhini chant forty-one times on the wall, but only nine times on the court?
Why did holding her breath for a minute at home not help her on the court?
Why did she keep her chant soft instead of shouting it?
Selvi Akka said, 'Now you know what the chant is for.' What do you think the chant is for?
What else do you do that is harder to do straight after running? Why?

A ten-year-old girl in a school sports shirt crossing the middle line at a run, mouth open in a gasp, while a young woman coach raises a whistle.
The same girl sitting under a wall clock at home with her cheeks puffed, holding her breath, while her grandmother shells peas beside her.

A girl sitting on a low wall with one foot up, counting on her fingers and whispering, with a surprised look.
The girl walking calmly to the middle line while seven defenders crouch and stare.
One quick lunge: the girl's fingertips on a defender's shoulder, her body already turning for home.

games.title: Which System? The organ card sort
games.context: This is a card game about the nine organ systems. You put each organ card on the mat of its system. Ten of the 24 organs belong on two mats, and finding the second mat earns a bonus point.

printables.title: 24 organ cards: the organ on the front, its system or systems and its job on the back

items.f: Skull: the bony case of the head
items.b: Skeletal. The skull protects the brain.

items.f: Thigh bone: the longest bone in the body
items.b: Skeletal and circulatory. The thigh bone holds you up, and the marrow inside makes blood cells.

items.f: Biceps: the muscle at the front of the upper arm
items.b: Muscular. The biceps bends the elbow. It is a voluntary muscle.

items.f: Diaphragm: a sheet of muscle under the lungs
items.b: Muscular and respiratory. The diaphragm is a muscle, and its pull draws air into the lungs.

items.f: Heart: in the chest, a little to the left
items.b: Circulatory and muscular. The heart pumps blood, and it is made of muscle that never rests.

items.f: Arteries and veins: tubes that reach every part of the body
items.b: Circulatory. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins carry it back.

items.f: Lungs: two spongy organs that fill the chest
items.b: Respiratory and excretory. The lungs take in oxygen, and they remove the waste gas carbon dioxide.

items.f: Windpipe: the ringed tube at the front of the neck
items.b: Respiratory. The windpipe carries air between the throat and the lungs.

items.f: Throat: the passage behind the nose and mouth
items.b: Digestive and respiratory. Food and air both pass through the throat.

items.f: Voice box: the bump at the front of the throat
items.b: Respiratory. The voice box sits at the top of the windpipe and makes the voice from breathed-out air.

items.f: Stomach: a stretchy bag under the left ribs
items.b: Digestive. The stomach churns food with acid.

items.f: Small intestine: a coiled tube several metres long in a grown-up
items.b: Digestive. Most food is digested here and passes into the blood.

items.f: Large intestine: the wider tube around the small intestine
items.b: Digestive. The large intestine takes water back from what is left of the food.

items.f: Liver: the heaviest organ inside the body, under the right ribs
items.b: Digestive and excretory. The liver makes bile to digest fat, and it turns protein waste into urea.

items.f: Pancreas: a soft organ behind the stomach
items.b: Digestive and hormone. The pancreas makes digestive juice, and it makes the hormones insulin and glucagon.

items.f: Kidneys: two bean-shaped organs at the back, under the ribs
items.b: Excretory and hormone. The kidneys make urine, and they make a hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells.

items.f: Bladder: a bag of muscle low in the belly
items.b: Excretory. The bladder stores urine until you pass it.

items.f: Brain: inside the skull
items.b: Nervous. The brain thinks, senses, starts movement and runs breathing and heartbeat.

items.f: Spinal cord: inside the backbone
items.b: Nervous. The spinal cord carries signals between the brain and the body.

items.f: Eye: in a bony socket of the skull
items.b: Nervous. The eye is a sense organ. It turns light into nerve signals.

items.f: Ovaries: two small organs low in the belly of a female body
items.b: Reproductive and hormone. The ovaries hold eggs, and they make hormones.

items.f: Testes: two small organs below the belly of a male body
items.b: Reproductive and hormone. The testes make sperm, and they make hormones.

items.f: Uterus: a bag of muscle low in the belly of a female body
items.b: Reproductive. A baby grows in the uterus, which is also called the womb.

items.f: Thyroid gland: a small gland at the front of the neck, below the voice box
items.b: Hormone. The thyroid makes a hormone that sets how fast cells use energy.

printables.title: A mat with nine spaces, one for each system
items: Hormone: slow messages in the blood

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, organ side up. Lay out the mat.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Put it on the mat of one system and say why. Then turn the card over.
If the back names that system, you score 1 point.
Some backs name a second system. You score 1 more point if you named it before you turned the card. If you did not, the next player may name it for the point.
With two players, take turns. With more, go round the circle.
Playing alone? Say one or two systems for each card, then turn the card over. The best possible score is 34.
After all 24 cards, the player with the most points wins.

setup.art: A paper mat with nine labelled spaces on a floor, and a pile of organ cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the mat. Put the pile organ side up.

setup.art: A child holding a card that says Pancreas over the space marked Digestive, with her other hand pointing to the space marked Hormone.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Put it on a system and say why. Name a second system if there is one.

setup.art: The card turned over to show its back, and a score sheet with tally marks.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check. Score your points.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards and the mat. 2. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, organ side up. 3. Read the nine spaces of the mat aloud together.
flow.say: Each card is an organ. Each space on the mat is an organ system. Some organs belong on two spaces, and those are worth a bonus.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the mat. Mix the cards. Read the nine systems aloud.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which System? You set up the organ cards and the mat of nine systems.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card. 2. Put it on a system and give a reason. 3. Name a second system if you think there is one. 4. Turn the card over and score.
flow.say: Read the card aloud. Which system is this organ in? Why? Does it also work for another system?
flow.kid: Read the card. Put it on a system. Say why. Name a second system if you can. Turn it over.

ask.q: Why does the thigh bone belong to the circulatory system as well as the skeleton?
good: The marrow inside makes blood cells.
Blood cells are part of the blood.

flow.parent: A good reason names the organ's job: 'the bladder stores urine, so it is excretory'. If your child argues for a system that is not on the back, listen. The tongue or the ribs could fairly be put in two places as well.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which System? You sort each organ card onto a system, and look for organs that belong on two.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Lay out all the cards with two systems on their backs. 3. Ask what these organs have in common.
flow.say: Count your points. Now put all the two-system cards in a row. How many are there? What does that tell you about the lists of systems?
flow.kid: Count your points. Find all the cards with two systems. How many are there?

check.q: In Which System?, 10 of the 24 organ cards belong on two mats. What does that show?
options: Many organs work for more than one system
The cards were printed wrongly
Those organs do no real work
check.why: An organ can do two different jobs, so it can sit on two lists. If you chose a printing mistake, look at the backs again: each one names two real jobs.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which System? You count the organs that belong to two systems.

games.title: Chain It: how many systems does one job need?
games.context: This is a talking game about systems working together. An event card names something a body does. Players take turns to name a system that helps and say what that system does.

printables.title: 12 event cards: the event on the front, the systems that help on the back

items.f: You run for the school bus.
items.b: Your nervous system decides to run and signals the muscles. Your muscular and skeletal systems move you. Your respiratory system takes in more oxygen, and your circulatory system carries it to the muscles. Your hormone system sends adrenaline.

items.f: You eat a masala dosa.
items.b: Your muscular system chews the food and squeezes it along. Your digestive system breaks the food down. Your circulatory system carries the sugar to the cells. Your hormone system sends insulin. Your nervous system gives you the taste and tells you when you are full.

items.f: You catch a steel tumbler as it falls.
items.b: Your nervous system sees the tumbler with the eye and signals the arm. Your muscular and skeletal systems move the arm. Your circulatory system brings the muscles their oxygen and food.

items.f: You sleep through the night.
items.b: Your respiratory system keeps breathing. Your circulatory system keeps the heart beating. Your nervous system, through the brainstem, runs both. Your excretory system keeps filtering the blood in the kidneys. Your hormone system sends growth hormone.

items.f: You stand in the hot May sun.
items.b: Your nervous system senses the heat. Your circulatory system sends blood to the skin to lose heat. Your excretory system sweats, and the kidneys save water. Your hormone system sends a message to the kidneys to save water.

items.f: You drink two tumblers of water.
items.b: Your digestive system takes the water into the blood through the gut wall. Your circulatory system carries it. Your excretory system lets the spare water out through the kidneys. Your hormone system tells the kidneys how much to let out. Your muscular system squeezes the bladder wall when you pass urine.

items.f: You sing a song.
items.b: Your respiratory system gives you the breath, and the voice box makes the sound. Your muscular system moves the diaphragm, tongue and lips. Your nervous system remembers the words and the tune. Your circulatory system feeds the brain and muscles.

items.f: A dog barks suddenly and you jump.
items.b: Your nervous system hears the bark with the ear, and the brain reacts. Your hormone system sends adrenaline. Your circulatory system speeds up the heart. Your muscular system makes you jump. Your respiratory system makes you breathe faster.

items.f: You climb to the third floor.
items.b: Your muscular and skeletal systems move your legs. Your respiratory and circulatory systems bring in the oxygen and carry it to the muscles. Your digestive system supplied the sugar at breakfast. Your excretory system lets the carbon dioxide leave through the lungs. Your nervous system keeps your balance.

items.f: A cut on your finger heals.
items.b: Your circulatory system makes the blood clot and brings repair cells. Your skeletal system helps, because the marrow made those cells. Your nervous system warns you with pain. Your digestive system supplies the building material.

items.f: You shiver on a cold morning in Ooty.
items.b: Your nervous system senses the cold. Your muscular system shivers, and shivering makes heat. Your circulatory system sends less blood to the skin to keep heat in. Your hormone system tells cells to burn more fuel.

items.f: You grow 5 centimetres in a year.
items.b: Your hormone system sends growth hormone. Your skeletal system lengthens the bones. Your digestive system supplies protein and calcium. Your circulatory system carries them to the bones. Your muscular system grows too.

printables.title: 9 system tokens, to remind players of the systems

rules: Lay the nine system tokens where everyone can see them. Put the event cards in a pile, event side up.
Turn over the top card and read the event aloud.
The first player names one system that helps with this event and says what it does. A token for that system is pushed forward.
The next player names a different system and says what it does. Go on round the players.
A player who cannot add a new system, or cannot say what it does, is out of that round. The last player still in wins the card.
If players disagree, read the back of the card. A system that is not on the back still counts if the player gives a good reason.
Playing alone? For each card, push forward every system you can explain. Then read the back. Score 1 point for each system you explained.
Play six cards. The player with the most cards wins.
