setup.caption: 1. Lay out the nine system tokens. Put the event cards in a pile.

setup.art: Two children and a mother at the table, one child pushing the token marked Respiratory forward while speaking.
setup.caption: 2. Take turns to name a system and say what it does for this event.

setup.art: An event card turned over to show the list of systems on its back.
setup.caption: 3. When nobody can add a system, read the back of the card.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 event cards and the 9 tokens. 2. Lay the tokens in a row. 3. Put the event cards in a pile, event side up.
flow.say: Each card is something your body does. We take turns to name a system that helps, and say what it does.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Lay the tokens in a row. Pile the event cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Chain It. You set up the event cards and the system tokens.

flow.do: 1. Turn over an event card and read it aloud. 2. Take turns to name a system and say what it does. 3. Push that token forward. 4. When nobody can add one, read the back. 5. Play six cards.
flow.say: Read the event. Name one system that helps, and say exactly what it does. Who can add another?
flow.kid: Read the event. Name a system that helps. Say what it does. Then the next player goes.

ask.q: Which system was named for almost every event? Why?
good: Circulatory, because every working organ needs blood.
Nervous, because something has to sense and signal.

flow.parent: Ask for the job, not only the name. 'Respiratory' alone is not enough. 'The lungs take in more oxygen' is.
flow.context: This is the main part of Chain It. You take turns to name the systems that help with each event.

flow.do: 1. Count the cards each player won. 2. Ask which event needed the most systems. 3. Ask whether any event needed only one.
flow.say: Which event needed the most systems? Was there any event that only one system could do alone?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which event needed the most systems? Did any need only one?

check.q: In Chain It, why does almost every event need the circulatory system?
options: Every working organ needs blood brought to it
The heart decides what the body does
Blood is the only thing the body needs
check.why: Blood brings oxygen and food to every organ and takes wastes away, so any job needs it. If you chose 'the heart decides', remember that the heart pumps but the deciding is done elsewhere.

flow.context: This is the last step of Chain It. You look back at how many systems each event needed.

experiments.title: One Breath Count: how long can you count aloud on one breath?
experiments.context: In this experiment you time how long you can count aloud on one breath. You do it sitting at rest, straight after one minute of step-ups, and again 1, 2 and 3 minutes later.
experiments.question: How long can you count aloud on one breath at rest? Does the time change straight after exercise? If it changes, how quickly does it come back?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will count aloud on one breath at rest, and again straight after one minute of step-ups. Will the second time be longer, shorter or the same? How many minutes will it take to come back? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: The same person counts every time, sitting down, in a normal talking voice, at the same speed. Start every count with one full breath in. Do the same step-ups for the same time, one minute, in both runs. Only one thing changes: how long ago the exercise ended. Do three tries at rest and two whole runs, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a phone with a stopwatch
a wall clock or a second phone, to see when each minute has passed
a low, firm step about 20 centimetres high, such as the bottom stair of the building. With no step, jog on the spot and lift your knees high
a chair or a floor mat to sit on
a notebook and a pencil
squared paper or a page from a maths notebook, for the line graph

experiments.safety: Use a low, firm step with nothing slippery on it, and keep a grown-up beside the child. Stop counting as soon as you need air, and never push on until you feel dizzy. Stop the step-ups at once if there is chest pain or wheezing. A child with asthma or a heart condition should do gentle marching on the spot and ask their doctor first.

schedule.what: Time three counts at rest. Do two runs of step-ups, and time a count straight after and at 1, 2 and 3 minutes. Find the averages and draw a line graph.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a line graph. Put the time since the step-ups along the bottom and the seconds of counting up the side. Mark your resting average as a line across the graph. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: seconds of counting on one breath
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair counting aloud with one hand on her chest, while a grown-up beside her holds a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still. Take one full breath and count aloud until you need air. Time it. Do this 3 times.

setup.art: The same child stepping up onto the bottom stair of a staircase, with a wall clock visible behind her.
setup.caption: 2. Do step-ups for 1 minute.

setup.art: The child sitting again, a little red in the face, counting aloud while the grown-up times her.
setup.caption: 3. Sit down and count on one breath straight away. Count again 1, 2 and 3 minutes later.

setup.art: A notebook with a line graph that drops low and then climbs back towards a dotted line marked 'at rest'.
setup.caption: 4. Do the whole run twice. Draw a line graph of the averages.

flow.do: 1. Explain the test. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write both in the notebook.
flow.say: We will time how long you can count aloud on one breath. First you sit still. Then you do step-ups for a minute and count again. Will the time be the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will count aloud on one breath. First at rest, then after step-ups. Will the times be the same? Why? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think the time will change, or stay the same?
good: After exercise I am out of breath, so I will need air sooner.
My lungs are the same size, so the time should be the same.
I breathe faster after running, so each breath is shorter.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. 'My lungs are the same size' is a sensible reason, and the test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the One Breath Count. You guess whether exercise will change how long you can count on one breath.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits quietly for 2 minutes. 2. They take one full breath in and count aloud at their usual talking speed. 3. Start the stopwatch on 'one'. Stop it when they need to breathe in. 4. Write the seconds. 5. Do this 3 times, with 1 minute of quiet breathing between tries.
flow.say: Take one full breath. Count aloud in your normal voice until you need air. Stop as soon as it stops being easy.
flow.kid: Sit still for two minutes. Take one big breath. Count aloud until you need air. Do this three times.
flow.parent: Most children of ten manage 12 to 25 seconds. The three tries often differ by 2 or 3 seconds. Keep the voice at talking loudness, because a loud voice uses air faster.

check.q: In the One Breath Count, why do you time three counts at rest and not just one?
options: One try can be a fluke
To make the lungs bigger
To get tired before the step-ups
check.why: Each try comes out a little different. The average of three is a fairer number to compare with. If you chose 'bigger lungs', remember that three breaths do not change the size of your lungs.

flow.context: In this step of the One Breath Count, you time three counts on one breath while sitting at rest.

flow.do: 1. Add the three resting times. 2. Divide by 3. 3. Write the answer in the table as the resting average.
flow.say: Add your three times and divide by 3. That average is the number we compare everything else with.
flow.kid: Add your three times. Divide by 3. Write the average in the table.
flow.context: In this step of the One Breath Count, you find the average of your three resting times.

flow.do: 1. Your child does step-ups on the bottom stair for 1 minute, as fast as is safe. 2. They sit down at once, take one full breath and count aloud. Time it. 3. Note the time on the wall clock when the step-ups ended. 4. They sit and breathe quietly. 5. They count again when 1 minute, 2 minutes and 3 minutes have passed. Time each count.
flow.say: Step up and down for one minute. Then sit, take one full breath and count. After that, breathe quietly. We will count again each minute.
flow.kid: Do step-ups for one minute. Sit down. Take one breath and count. Count again after 1, 2 and 3 minutes.
flow.parent: The first count after the step-ups is often only 4 to 8 seconds. Your child may be surprised and want to try again. Write down the first try, because that is the honest result.
flow.context: In this step of the One Breath Count, you do one minute of step-ups. Then you time a count straight away and at 1, 2 and 3 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Your child rests in the chair for 5 minutes. 2. Repeat the whole run: 1 minute of step-ups, then a count straight away and at 1, 2 and 3 minutes. 3. Write these times in the Run 2 column.
flow.say: Rest for five minutes. Then we do the whole run once more. Two runs tell us more than one.
flow.kid: Rest for five minutes. Then do the whole run again. Write the new times.
flow.context: In this step of the One Breath Count, you rest and then repeat the run of step-ups and counts.

flow.do: 1. For each row, add Run 1 and Run 2 and halve the answer. 2. Draw a line graph of the averages. 3. Draw a straight line across the graph at the resting average.
flow.say: Find the average for each row. Then plot the points and join them. Where is the line lowest? When does it get back to your resting line?
flow.kid: Find the average for each row. Plot the points. Join them with a line.
flow.context: In this step of the One Breath Count, you draw a line graph of your average counting times.

flow.do: 1. Look at the graph together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your graph. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Your lungs stayed the same size. So what changed?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Your lungs were the same size in every count. So why was the count so short straight after the step-ups?
good: My body needed fresh air sooner.
My muscles had used a lot of oxygen.
I could not hold the air in for long, because I had to breathe.

ask.q: Where does the air for your voice come from?
good: From my lungs, when I breathe out.
It is the same air I breathe.

flow.parent: Straight after the step-ups, most children count for a third of their resting time or less. They are nearly back after 3 minutes. Write what you really found. The reason: the voice is made in the voice box, at the top of the windpipe. Air leaving the lungs shakes two folds there. So you can speak only while breathing out, and no fresh air comes in while you speak. During the step-ups the muscles used oxygen and made carbon dioxide. The brainstem measures carbon dioxide in the blood. When there is more, it forces the next breath sooner. So breathing and speaking share one stream of air, and after exercise the breathing takes it first.
flow.think: A kabaddi raider must chant 'kabaddi' on one breath for the whole raid. Why does the rule make running harder?
flow.context: This is the last step of the One Breath Count. You say what your graph shows and why counting was so short after the step-ups.

experiments.title: Beans and Threes: can your brain do two hard jobs at once?
experiments.context: In this experiment you move beans from one bowl to another while counting backwards in threes. You find out whether your brain can do two jobs at once without slowing down. You also find out whether the kind of job matters.
experiments.question: You move beans and count backwards in threes at the same time. Do you do each job as well as when you do it alone? Is it different if the second job is singing a song you know by heart?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will move beans alone, count backwards alone, and then do both together. Will you move as many beans when you also count? Will singing a song slow the beans as much as counting does? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every round lasts 30 seconds. Use the same hand, the same two bowls and the same gap of about 20 centimetres between them. Move one bean at a time. Rest for half a minute between rounds. Do every kind of round twice. The second time, start counting from 101 and not 100, so that the answers are new. Only one thing changes: what else the brain is doing.

materials.item: rajma, chana or other large beans
small bowls or steel tumblers
a phone with a stopwatch
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows: beans alone, threes alone, beans with threes, and beans with a song. Write the beans moved and the right answers for both tries.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Two small steel bowls about 20 centimetres apart on a table, one holding a heap of rajma beans and one empty.
setup.caption: 1. Put 40 beans in one bowl. Put the empty bowl 20 centimetres away.

setup.art: A child moving one bean with finger and thumb from one bowl to the other while a grown-up watches a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Move beans one at a time for 30 seconds. Count how many you moved.

setup.art: The same child moving a bean with her mouth open, saying a number, while the grown-up ticks a list of numbers in a notebook.
setup.caption: 3. Now move beans and count backwards in threes at the same time.

setup.art: A notebook table with four rows of results.
setup.caption: 4. Do every kind of round twice. Compare the numbers.

flow.do: 1. Show the bowls and the beans. 2. Explain the four kinds of round. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: You will move beans, count backwards in threes, and then do both at once. Will you still move as many beans? Will singing slow you as much as counting? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will move beans and count backwards. First alone, then together. Will the beans slow down? Why?

good: My hands and my mouth are different parts, so both can work.
I can only think about one thing at a time.
Singing is easy, so it will not slow me.

flow.parent: Write the list of right answers in the notebook before you start: 100, 97, 94, 91, 88, 85, 82, 79, 76, 73, 70, 67. For the second try: 101, 98, 95, 92, 89, 86, 83, 80, 77, 74, 71, 68.
flow.context: This is the first step of Beans and Threes. You guess whether doing two jobs at once will slow you down.

flow.do: 1. Beans alone: your child moves beans one at a time for 30 seconds. Count the beans moved. 2. Rest for half a minute. 3. Threes alone: your child counts backwards from 100 in threes, aloud, for 30 seconds. Tick each right answer on your list.
flow.say: Move the beans one at a time, as fast as you can. Stop when I say stop. Next, count backwards from 100 in threes, aloud.
flow.kid: Move beans for 30 seconds. Count them. Rest. Then count backwards from 100 in threes.
flow.context: In this step of Beans and Threes, you do each job alone for 30 seconds: moving beans, and counting backwards in threes.

flow.do: 1. Beans with threes: your child moves beans and counts backwards from 100 in threes at the same time, for 30 seconds. Count the beans and tick the right answers. 2. Rest for half a minute. 3. Beans with a song: your child moves beans while singing a song they know by heart, for 30 seconds. Count the beans.
flow.say: Now do both at once. Keep moving beans and keep counting backwards. After a rest, move beans again while you sing a song you know well.
flow.kid: Move beans and count backwards together. Rest. Then move beans while you sing.
flow.parent: Watch the hand. Many children stop the hand for a moment each time they work out a number. That pause is worth pointing out afterwards.
flow.context: In this step of Beans and Threes, you move beans while counting backwards. Then you move beans while singing a song you know by heart.

flow.do: 1. Repeat all four rounds. 2. This time start the counting from 101. 3. Write every number in the table.
flow.say: We do all four rounds once more, starting from 101 this time. Then we can see whether the first result was a fluke.
flow.kid: Do all four rounds again. Start counting from 101 this time. Write every number.
flow.context: In this step of Beans and Threes, you repeat all four rounds so that you have two tries of each.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at the numbers. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which second job slowed the beans more? Did your breathing stop in any round?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Why did counting backwards slow the beans more than singing did?
good: Counting backwards needs thinking, and so does picking up each bean.
I know the song by heart, so I do not have to think about it.

ask.q: Which jobs did your body keep doing in every round, without slowing?
good: Breathing.
My heart kept beating.
I kept sitting upright.

flow.parent: In most children, both numbers fall when the two jobs are done together. The beans often fall by a quarter or more. A song known by heart hardly slows the beans. Write what you really found. The reason: picking up a small bean and taking away three both need attention from the cerebrum. The cerebrum switches between two hard jobs, and each switch costs time. A song known by heart needs little attention. All the while, the brainstem ran the breathing and the heartbeat without a pause. Scientists still argue about exactly what limits attention.
flow.think: Why is it dangerous for a driver to read a phone message, even on an empty road?
flow.context: This is the last step of Beans and Threes. You say what your numbers show about doing two jobs at once.

experiments.title: The Swallow Pause: what does your breathing do when you swallow?
experiments.context: In this experiment you feel your own breath on a wet finger while you swallow sips of water. You find out whether breathing stops for a swallow, and whether you breathe in or out straight afterwards.
experiments.question: Does your breathing stop when you swallow? Straight after a swallow, is your first breath in or out?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When you swallow a sip of water, does your breathing carry on or stop? Straight after the swallow, will you breathe in first or out first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Take ten small sips of the same size. Sit upright every time. Breathe through your nose in your normal way, and take two or three breaths between sips. Do not try to control your breathing. Count all ten swallows, even the ones that surprise you.
results_table: Did the air stop? (yes or no)
First air after the swallow (out or in)

materials.item: a tumbler of drinking water
a steel spoon, cooled in the fridge for 10 minutes (the grown-up may use it to watch for mist)
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Sit upright and take small sips. Never try to breathe in while there is water in your mouth. In the last part, use only your own saliva.
experiments.record: Make a tally of ten swallows: how many times the air stopped, and how many times the first air afterwards was out.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results for ten swallows
rows: The air stopped during the swallow
First air after the swallow was out
First air after the swallow was in
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child sitting upright at a table, one wet finger held level just under her nostrils, a tumbler of water in her other hand.
setup.caption: 1. Wet one finger. Hold it just under your nose. Feel the warm air out and the cool air in.

setup.art: The child swallowing a sip with the finger still under her nose, while a grown-up makes tally marks in a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Take a small sip and swallow. Feel what the air does. Say 'out' or 'in' for the first air afterwards.

setup.art: A notebook page with ten tally rows and two columns.
setup.caption: 3. Do ten sips. Count the tallies.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess and a reason. 2. Write both down. 3. Your child wets one finger and holds it under their nostrils, with the mouth closed.
flow.say: When you swallow, does your breathing carry on or stop? After the swallow, do you breathe in or out first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Does your breath stop when you swallow? What comes next, in or out? Why? Write your guess.

good: I think it stops, or water would go into my lungs.
I think I breathe in after, because I missed a breath.
I think I breathe out, to push the water away.

flow.parent: On a wet finger, air breathed out feels warm and air breathed in feels cool. Let your child practise for a few breaths until they can tell the two apart.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Swallow Pause. You guess what your breathing does during and after a swallow.

flow.do: 1. Your child takes a small sip and swallows, with the wet finger under the nose. 2. They say whether the air stopped, and whether the first air afterwards was out or in. 3. Tally it. 4. They take two or three normal breaths. 5. Do this for ten sips.
flow.say: Take a small sip and swallow. Did the air stop? Was the first air afterwards warm, going out, or cool, coming in?
flow.kid: Take a small sip. Swallow. Did the air stop? Was the next air out or in? Do ten sips.
flow.parent: You can check with the cold spoon. Hold it just under your child's nose. Mist appears on the steel when they breathe out. If the feeling is hard to judge, write a question mark for that swallow.
flow.context: In this step of the Swallow Pause, you swallow ten small sips and feel what your breathing does each time.

flow.do: 1. Put the water away. 2. Your child tries three times to swallow their own saliva and breathe in at the same moment. 3. Ask what happened.
flow.say: Now, with no water, try to swallow and breathe in at the same moment. Try three times. What happens?
flow.kid: Put the water away. Try to swallow and breathe in together. Try three times.

check.q: In the Swallow Pause, why can you not breathe in while you swallow?
options: The windpipe is covered during a swallow
The lungs are full of water
The nose closes when the mouth opens
check.why: During a swallow the voice box lifts and the epiglottis folds over the windpipe, so no air can pass. If you chose the lungs, remember that the cover is there to keep water out of them.

flow.context: In this step of the Swallow Pause, you try to swallow and breathe in at the same moment. You use only saliva.

flow.do: 1. Count the tallies. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Count your tallies. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Count your tallies. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: Why might breathing out be the safer first breath after a swallow?
good: It blows any last drops away from the windpipe.
Breathing in could pull drops into the lungs.

flow.parent: The air stops at every swallow, for about one second. In studies of grown-ups, the first breath afterwards is usually out. Children vary more, so write what you really found. The reason: the throat is shared by air and food. During a swallow, the brainstem stops the breathing, the voice box lifts and the epiglottis covers the windpipe. Scientists think breathing out afterwards helps to clear any drops left near the opening.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Swallow Pause. You count your tallies and say what they show about breathing and swallowing.

activities.title: Say It While You Swallow: three things to notice in your throat
activities.context: This is a short activity to notice what your throat does, before you learn about it. You feel a swallow with your fingers and try to make a sound while you swallow. You also hum with your nose pinched.

materials.item: your own throat, nose and voice
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Use only your own saliva for the swallows. Do not try this with food or water in your mouth.
activities.record: Write two things you noticed and two questions you now have.

setup.art: A child resting two fingers lightly on the front of her throat while she swallows, with a small arrow showing a bump moving up.
setup.caption: 1. Rest two fingers on the front of your throat. Swallow. Feel the bump move.

setup.art: A child with her mouth open in a long 'aaaa' sound.
setup.caption: 2. Say a long 'aaaa'. Swallow in the middle of it.

setup.art: A child humming with her lips closed and pinching her nose shut with two fingers.
setup.caption: 3. Hum with your lips closed. Then pinch your nose.

flow.do: 1. Your child rests two fingers lightly on the front of the throat. 2. They swallow their own saliva. 3. Ask what the fingers felt.
flow.say: Rest two fingers on the front of your throat. Now swallow. What did the bump under your fingers do?
flow.kid: Put two fingers on the front of your throat. Swallow. What does the bump do?
flow.parent: The bump is the voice box. It jumps up and drops back with every swallow. Do not explain yet. Only ask what your child felt.
flow.context: This is the first step of Say It While You Swallow. You feel what the front of your throat does during a swallow.

flow.do: 1. Your child says one long, steady 'aaaa'. 2. In the middle of the sound, they swallow. 3. Try it three times.
flow.say: Say a long 'aaaa' and keep it going. Now swallow in the middle. Could you keep the sound going through the swallow?
flow.kid: Say a long 'aaaa'. Swallow in the middle. Did the sound keep going?
flow.context: This step of Say It While You Swallow tests whether you can make a sound and swallow together.

flow.do: 1. Your child hums with lips closed. 2. While humming, they pinch the nose shut. 3. Ask what happened to the hum.
flow.say: Hum with your lips closed. Keep humming and pinch your nose shut. What happens to the hum?
flow.kid: Hum with your lips closed. Now pinch your nose. What happens to the hum?
flow.parent: The hum stops within a second. With the lips and the nose both shut, the air has no way out. A voice needs air that is moving.
flow.context: In this step of Say It While You Swallow, you hum with your lips closed and then pinch your nose.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child noticed and what they wonder. 2. Write two questions in the notebook. 3. Keep them for the end of the unit.
flow.say: What did you notice in these three tries? What do you wonder about your throat and your voice?
flow.kid: What did you notice? What do you wonder? Write two questions.

good: Why does my voice stop when I swallow?
Why does the hum need my nose?
What is the bump that moves?

flow.parent: Do not answer the questions yet. The One Breath Count, the Swallow Pause and the cards on shared organs answer them.
flow.context: This is the last step of Say It While You Swallow. You write down what you noticed and what you wonder.

activities.title: The Hundred Beans: where does the blood go when you run?
activities.context: In this activity each bean stands for one small tumbler of blood pumped in a minute. You share the beans among the organs, first for a body at rest and then for a body running hard.

materials.item: rajma, chana or any large beans
small bowls, or slips of paper to mark seven places on the floor
a pen and seven paper labels: Muscles, Gut and liver, Kidneys, Brain, Skin, Heart muscle, Everything else
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Draw a table with seven rows, one for each place. Write your guess and the real number of beans, at rest and in hard exercise.

example_chart.title: Blood pumped each minute in a grown-up, in beans. One bean is 200 millilitres
example_chart.note: These are rounded figures for a grown-up, taken from textbooks of how the body works. Real bodies differ.

setup.art: Seven small steel bowls in a row on the floor, each with a paper label, and a heap of rajma beans beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Label seven bowls. Count out 25 beans for a body at rest.

setup.art: A child dropping beans into the bowls, with most beans going into the bowls marked Gut and liver, Kidneys and Muscles.
setup.caption: 2. Guess how the 25 beans are shared. Then put them where they really go.

setup.art: The same bowls, with the bowl marked Muscles now heaped with beans and the others almost empty.
setup.caption: 3. Count out 100 beans for hard exercise. Guess, then share them out.

flow.do: 1. Label the seven bowls. 2. Count out 25 beans. 3. Ask your child to share them among the bowls as a guess, and to give a reason.
flow.say: At rest, a grown-up's heart pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute. Each bean is 200 millilitres, so that is 25 beans. Which organs get the most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Each bean is one small tumbler of blood. Share 25 beans among the bowls. Which organ gets most? Why?

ask.q: Why did you give that bowl the most?
good: The brain never stops, so it needs a lot.
Muscles are the biggest part of the body.
The heart works hardest.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Hundred Beans. You guess how the blood is shared among the organs of a body at rest.

flow.do: 1. Read out the real shares at rest. 2. Your child moves the beans to match. Gut and liver 6, kidneys 5, muscles 5, brain 4, skin 2, heart muscle 1, everything else 2. 3. Write the guess and the real number side by side.
flow.say: Here are the real shares. Gut and liver 6, kidneys 5, muscles 5, brain 4, skin 2, heart muscle 1, everything else 2. Which one surprises you most?
flow.kid: Move the beans to the real shares. Which bowl surprises you most?
flow.parent: The kidneys usually surprise children most. Two organs the size of a fist take a fifth of the blood. All the blood must be filtered again and again.
flow.context: In this step of the Hundred Beans, you set out the real shares of blood at rest. Then you compare them with your guess.

flow.do: 1. Count out 75 more beans, to make 100. 2. Tell your child the body is now running hard. 3. Ask them to share all 100 beans as a guess. 4. Ask whether any bowl should get fewer beans than before, and why.
flow.say: In hard exercise the heart pumps about 20 litres a minute. That is 100 beans. Where do they go now? Does any organ get fewer beans than at rest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Now the body runs hard. Share 100 beans. Does any bowl get fewer than before? Why?
flow.context: In this step of the Hundred Beans, you guess how the blood is shared when the body is running hard.

flow.do: 1. Read out the real shares in hard exercise. 2. Your child moves the beans to match. Muscles 80, skin 6, brain 4, heart muscle 4, gut and liver 2, kidneys 2, everything else 2. 3. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Here are the real shares. Muscles 80, skin 6, brain 4, heart muscle 4, gut and liver 2, kidneys 2, everything else 2. Compare each bowl with the rest round.
flow.kid: Move the beans to the real shares. Compare each bowl with before.
flow.context: In this step of the Hundred Beans, you set out the real shares of blood in hard exercise.

flow.do: 1. Ask which bowls got fewer beans, which got the same and which got more. 2. Ask for a reason for each. 3. Read the note below after your child has answered.
flow.say: Which organs got less blood than at rest? Which got the same? Why would the skin get more?
flow.kid: Which bowls got fewer beans? Which got the same? Why did the skin get more?

check.q: In the Hundred Beans, the brain has 4 beans at rest and 4 in hard exercise. What does this tell you?
options: The brain gets about the same amount of blood
The brain gets four times as much blood
The brain stops working in exercise
check.why: Four beans is 800 millilitres a minute in both rounds. The brain's supply is kept steady while the supply to other organs changes. If you chose 'four times', check the beans: the total grew four times, but the brain's bowl did not.

flow.parent: Blood vessels in the gut and the kidneys narrow, and vessels in the muscles widen. So the gut and the kidneys get less than half of what they had, and digestion slows. The skin gets more because the blood carries heat there to be lost. The brain's supply stays the same. These figures are for a grown-up. A child's heart pumps less, but the pattern is the same.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Hundred Beans. You compare the two rounds and say why the blood is shared differently.

activities.title: Your Largest Organ: measure your skin with one hand
activities.context: In this activity you find the area of your hand by counting squares. Doctors use the rule that one hand covers about one hundredth of a person's skin. You use the rule to work out how much skin you have.

materials.item: plain paper, about A4 size
a ruler and a sharp pencil
one open double page of a newspaper

activities.record: Write the area of your hand in square centimetres and the area of your skin. Write how many newspaper pages your skin would cover.

setup.art: A sheet of paper ruled into one-centimetre squares, with a ruler and a pencil beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Rule the paper into squares 1 centimetre wide.

setup.art: A child's hand lying flat on the squared paper with fingers together, a pencil line traced round it.
setup.caption: 2. Lay your hand flat with the fingers together. Trace round it to the wrist.

setup.art: The traced hand shape with a dot in each counted square and a number written beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Count the squares inside. Multiply by 100.

flow.do: 1. Rule lines 1 centimetre apart across the paper, and then down it. 2. Cover a patch at least 20 centimetres long and 12 centimetres wide. 3. Check a few squares with the ruler.
flow.say: First we make squared paper. Each square is 1 centimetre long and 1 centimetre wide, so its area is 1 square centimetre.
flow.kid: Rule lines 1 centimetre apart, across and down. Each square is 1 square centimetre.
flow.parent: A squared maths notebook saves time, but measure its squares first. If they are not 1 centimetre wide, rule your own.
flow.context: This is the first step of Your Largest Organ. You make squared paper so that you can measure the area of your hand.

flow.do: 1. Your child lays one hand flat on the squares, palm down, fingers and thumb together. 2. Trace round the hand, and close the shape at the wrist crease. 3. Count every whole square inside. 4. Count a part square as one if half or more is inside. Leave out smaller parts.
flow.say: Trace round your hand. Now count the squares inside. Put a dot in each one you count, so that none is counted twice.
flow.kid: Lay your hand flat. Trace round it. Count the squares inside. Dot each one you count.
flow.parent: A child of ten usually counts between 85 and 115 squares. A grown-up counts between 140 and 190.
flow.context: In this step of Your Largest Organ, you trace your hand on squared paper. Then you count the squares to find its area.

flow.do: 1. Multiply the hand's area by 100. That is roughly the area of all the skin. 2. Compare the answer with 10,000 square centimetres, which is 1 square metre. 3. Measure the length and width of the open newspaper page and multiply them. 4. Work out how many such pages the skin would cover.
flow.say: One hand covers about one hundredth of your skin. So multiply by 100. Is your skin more or less than 1 square metre? How many newspaper pages is that?
flow.kid: Multiply your hand's area by 100. That is about all your skin. How many newspaper pages is it?

ask.q: Why is this only a rough answer?
good: The rule of one hundredth is itself rough.
I rounded the part squares.
People have different shapes.

flow.parent: Doctors use this rule to judge how much skin a burn covers. It is a rough rule. For a child of ten the answer is usually close to 1 square metre. That is between two and three open newspaper pages.
flow.context: In this step of Your Largest Organ, you multiply the area of your hand by 100. The answer is roughly the area of your skin.

flow.do: 1. Ask what the skin does for the body. 2. List the jobs together. 3. Ask which organ systems the skin helps.
flow.say: Your skin is usually called your largest organ. What jobs does it do? Which organ systems does it help?
flow.kid: What jobs does your skin do? Which organ systems does it help?

check.q: Which of these is a job of the skin?
options: Losing heat by sweating
Pumping blood
Digesting food
check.why: Sweat carries heat away as it dries. The skin also keeps water in and germs out, senses touch and heat, and makes vitamin D in sunlight. Pumping is the heart's job, and digesting is the gut's.

flow.parent: The skin keeps water in and germs out. It senses touch, heat, cold and pain, so it works with the nervous system. It sweats out water and salt, so it helps the excretory system. It makes vitamin D in sunlight. A grown-up's skin weighs about 4 kilograms.
flow.context: This is the last step of Your Largest Organ. You list the jobs of the skin and the systems it helps.

activities.title: The Handover Map: draw what each system gives the next
activities.context: In this activity you draw one job, climbing three floors of stairs, as a map of boxes and arrows. Each arrow shows what one organ hands to another: oxygen, sugar, carbon dioxide, heat or a signal.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper, such as the back of an old calendar page
a pencil and three colour pencils

activities.record: Keep the finished map. Under it, write which box you think the body could least do without, and why.

setup.art: A large sheet of paper with eight boxes drawn in a ring, labelled Brain and nerves, Leg muscles and bones, Lungs, Heart and blood, Small intestine, Liver, Skin, Kidneys.
setup.caption: 1. Draw eight boxes in a ring and label them.

setup.art: The same sheet with arrows between the boxes, each arrow labelled with a word such as oxygen, sugar, heat or signal.
setup.caption: 2. Draw an arrow for each handover. Write on the arrow what is handed over.

setup.art: A child's hand covering one box on the map while she points at the arrows that leave it.
setup.caption: 3. Cover one box with your hand. Say what would stop.

flow.do: 1. Write the job at the top: 'Climb three floors of stairs'. 2. Draw eight boxes in a ring. 3. Label them: Brain and nerves, Leg muscles and bones, Lungs, Heart and blood, Small intestine, Liver, Skin, Kidneys.
flow.say: We will draw everything your body does to climb three floors. Each box is an organ or a pair of organs.
flow.kid: Write the job at the top. Draw eight boxes in a ring. Label them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Handover Map. You draw eight boxes for the organs that help you climb stairs.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what the leg muscles need, and where each thing comes from. 2. For each answer, draw an arrow between two boxes. 3. Write on the arrow what is handed over. 4. Use one colour for things carried in the blood, one for nerve signals and one for wastes and heat.
flow.say: What do your leg muscles need in order to work? Where does each thing come from? What do the muscles give back?
flow.kid: What do your leg muscles need? Where does it come from? Draw an arrow for each handover.

ask.q: What do working muscles hand back to the blood?
good: Carbon dioxide.
Heat.
Other wastes.

flow.parent: A full map has at least these arrows. The brain sends signals to the muscles. The lungs pass oxygen to the blood. The small intestine passes sugar from breakfast to the blood. The liver passes stored sugar to the blood. The blood carries oxygen and sugar to the muscles. The muscles hand carbon dioxide and heat back to the blood. The blood carries carbon dioxide to the lungs and heat to the skin. The blood carries urea and spare water to the kidneys. The blood tells the brain how much carbon dioxide there is. The brain then sends signals to the heart and lungs to work faster.
flow.context: In this step of the Handover Map, you draw an arrow for each thing that one organ hands to another.

flow.do: 1. Your child covers one box with a hand. 2. Ask what would stop first if that organ stopped working. 3. Try three different boxes.
flow.say: Cover the lungs with your hand. Follow the arrows. What stops first? Now try the liver, and then the heart.
flow.kid: Cover one box. Follow the arrows. What stops first? Try three boxes.
flow.context: In this step of the Handover Map, you cover one organ at a time. You work out what would stop without it.

flow.do: 1. In a corner of the map, sketch the heart as four boxes: two above and two below. 2. Your child traces the path of the blood with a finger and says each chamber aloud.

check.q: Blood leaves the right ventricle. Where does it go next?
options: To the lungs
To the legs
To the left ventricle
check.why: The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen. The blood then returns to the left atrium. If you chose the left ventricle, remember that a wall divides the two sides of the heart.

projects.title: The Layer Book: nine systems on see-through pages
projects.context: In this three-day project you draw the organ systems on see-through pages, a few systems to a page. Then you stack the pages over one body outline and look for organs that appear on two pages.

materials.item: plain paper, about A4 size, for the body outline
tracing paper or butter paper, cut to the same size. Thin white paper held against a bright window also works
a pencil and five colour pencils
a stapler, or a needle and thread, to join the pages at the top
the picture cards in this unit, or any school book with pictures of the organs, to copy from

schedule.what: Draw the body outline. On page 1, draw the main bones, the biceps and the diaphragm.
On page 2, draw the digestive system. On page 3, draw the respiratory and circulatory systems.
On page 4, draw the excretory and reproductive systems. On page 5, draw the nervous and hormone systems. Stack the pages and star the shared organs.

projects.record: A book of one outline and five see-through pages. On the last page, write a list of every organ you drew on two pages.

setup.caption: 2. Lay a see-through page on the outline. Draw one or two systems on it.

flow.do: 1. Day 1. Draw a body outline on the plain paper, from the head to the knees, as large as the page allows. 2. Lay page 1 over it. 3. In one colour, draw the skull, backbone, ribs, hip bones, and arm and thigh bones. 4. In a second colour, add the biceps on one arm and the diaphragm under the ribs. 5. Label each part.

flow.kid: Draw a body outline. Lay page 1 on it. Draw the main bones, the biceps and the diaphragm.
flow.parent: Simple shapes are enough. What matters is that each organ sits in the right place: the diaphragm as a curved line under the ribs, the hip bones as a bowl.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Layer Book. You draw the body outline and the first see-through page, with bones and muscles.

flow.do: 1. Day 2. On page 2, draw the digestive system: mouth, throat, food pipe, stomach, small and large intestine, liver and pancreas. 2. On page 3, draw the nose, throat, voice box, windpipe, lungs and diaphragm in one colour. 3. On the same page, draw the heart with its four chambers and the main blood vessels in another colour. 4. Label each part.

flow.kid: On page 2, draw the digestive system. On page 3, draw the lungs and the heart. Label each part.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you draw the bones
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Layer Book. You draw the digestive system on one page and the respiratory and circulatory systems on another.

flow.do: 1. Day 3. On page 4, draw the kidneys, ureters and bladder, and the reproductive organs. 2. On page 5, draw the brain in three parts, the spinal cord, and the glands: thyroid, adrenals, pancreas, and ovaries or testes. 3. Stack all five pages over the outline and staple them at the top. 4. Look through the stack. Put a star by every organ that appears on two pages.
flow.say: Today you finish the book. Hold the stack up to the light. Which organs did you draw twice? Why did you have to?
flow.kid: Draw pages 4 and 5. Stack all the pages. Star each organ that you drew on two pages.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you draw the lungs and the heart

ask.q: Which organs did you draw on two pages, and why?
good: The throat, because air and food both pass through.
The diaphragm, because it is a muscle and it does the breathing.
The pancreas, because it makes digestive juice and hormones.
The ovaries or testes, because they also make hormones.

flow.parent: Your child may also notice that the ribs help with breathing, and that the marrow in the bones makes blood. Any organ with a reason counts.

challenges.title: The Throat Switch: one way in, two ways down
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge about the shared throat. In Say It While You Swallow, you felt your voice box jump up at every swallow. Here you build a model throat that sends food one way and air the other.
challenges.problem: Build a model throat with one opening at the top and two cups below: a stomach cup and a lung cup. Rajma beans are the food, and small paper balls are the air. Every bean must land in the stomach cup, and every paper ball must land in the lung cup.
constraints: Everything goes in through the same opening at the top.
Once a bean or a paper ball is dropped, you may not touch either one.
In your first design you may pull one thread to work a flap.
Test with 10 beans and 10 paper balls, dropped in a mixed-up order.
materials: cardboard from an old carton or cereal box
10 small balls of crumpled paper, each about the size of a bean
a cardboard tube, or a tube rolled from old chart paper
general: A flap on a tape hinge covers the way to the lung cup. Pull a thread to close it for each bean, as the epiglottis does.
Move the lung tube instead of the flap. Slide it up under a fixed roof for each bean, as your voice box lifts when you swallow.
Use a sloping ramp with a gate that you swing to one side or the other.
creative: Make the switch work by weight. A light flap lets a heavy bean drop through, but a paper ball rolls across it to the lung cup.
Build a whale's design: two separate openings and no switch at all. Then say what a whale gives up.
Add a puff test. Blow down the top and check that the air comes out on the lung side.
challenges.your_turn: Now design a throat that needs no thread. It must sort beans from paper balls with no help from you. Draw it, build it and test it with 10 beans and 10 paper balls. Write how many went the right way.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Recall Say It While You Swallow, where the bump in the throat jumped up at each swallow. 3. Ask what the real throat does to keep food out of the windpipe.
flow.say: In Say It While You Swallow, your voice box jumped up at every swallow. What was it doing? How could a model do the same job?
flow.kid: Your voice box jumped up when you swallowed. Why? How could a model do that job?

ask.q: What stops food going down the windpipe?
good: A flap covers it.
The voice box lifts up under the flap.
Breathing stops for a moment.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Throat Switch. You recall what your own throat does in a swallow, and plan a model.

flow.do: 1. Tape the tube upright on the cardboard, above the two cups. 2. Cut a card flap and hinge it with tape below the tube. 3. Tie the thread to the flap. 4. Try a few beans and paper balls, and adjust the flap.
flow.say: Build your first design. Where should the hinge go, so that the flap covers the lung side when you pull?
flow.kid: Fix the tube above the cups. Add a flap and a thread. Try a few beans.
flow.parent: Cardboard is hard to cut, so a grown-up should help with the scissors. A flap about 5 centimetres long, hinged at its top edge, is easy to steer.
flow.context: In this step of the Throat Switch, you build a model throat with a flap worked by a thread.

flow.do: 1. Mix 10 beans and 10 paper balls in a bowl. 2. Your child drops them one at a time and works the thread. 3. Tally where each one lands. 4. Change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Drop them in a mixed-up order. How many went the right way? What one thing will you change?
flow.kid: Drop 10 beans and 10 paper balls. Tally where they land. Change one thing and test again.

check.q: A bean lands in the lung cup. In a real throat, what would happen next?
options: A cough to blow it back out
Nothing at all
The stomach would move up
check.why: Anything that touches the inside of the windpipe sets off a cough, which blasts air out to clear it. If you chose 'nothing', remember how hard you cough when a drop of water 'goes down the wrong way'.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Throat Switch. You test your model throat with beans and paper balls, and improve it.

worksheets.title: The organ systems and their organs (core)

items.p: Which list names organs of one organ system?
items.why: The mouth, stomach, intestines and liver all work on digesting food. The other lists mix organs from different systems.

items.p: Put these in the order that breathed-in air passes through them.
items.why: Air enters by the nose and crosses the throat. It goes down the windpipe and through the bronchi to the alveoli.

items.p: Match each organ system to its job.
items.why: Each system has one big job for the whole body. The blood carries, the kidneys remove wastes, the bones hold the body up and the nerves signal.

items.p: The two lower chambers of the heart, which pump blood out, are called ____.
items.why: The atria at the top receive blood. The ventricles below pump it out to the lungs and to the body.

items.p: Blood passes through the heart twice on each full trip round the body.
items.why: True. The right side pumps blood to the lungs. The blood comes back, and the left side pumps it to the body.

items.p: Sort these muscles. Is each one voluntary or involuntary?
items.why: You choose when to move your arm, tongue and legs. The heart, the stomach and the intestines work without your choosing.

items.p: Which part of the brain keeps your balance and makes movement smooth?
items.why: The cerebellum sits at the back, under the cerebrum. Choosing the cerebrum is a common slip, because the names sound alike. The cerebrum does the thinking.

items.p: Put these in the order that urine passes through them.
items.why: The kidney makes urine. A ureter carries it to the bladder, which stores it. Urine leaves through the urethra.

items.p: The liver stores sugar as well as making bile.
items.why: True. The liver stores sugar as glycogen and releases it into the blood between meals. It has many jobs.

items.p: A baby begins when a sperm joins an ____.
items.why: The egg comes from an ovary and the sperm from a testis. The joined cell divides and grows in the uterus.

items.p: Label the four chambers of the heart on this drawing.
a: Right atrium: upper chamber, receives blood from the body
Right ventricle: lower chamber, pumps blood to the lungs
Left atrium: upper chamber, receives blood from the lungs
Left ventricle: lower chamber, pumps blood to the body
items.why: The atria are on top and the ventricles below. In a drawing, the heart's right side is on the left of the page, as if the person faces you.
items.art: A simple front view of a heart cut open to show four chambers, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Name two organs that work in two organ systems. Give both jobs of each organ.
items.a: For example: the throat carries air to the lungs and food to the stomach. The pancreas makes digestive juice and also makes the hormone insulin.
items.why: A strong answer names two real organs and gives two different jobs for each. The thigh bone, the diaphragm, the liver and the kidneys are other good choices.

items.p: Straight after step-ups, you can count for far less time on one breath. Explain why.
items.a: The voice uses air that is leaving the lungs. After step-ups the muscles have used oxygen and made carbon dioxide. The body must breathe in fresh air sooner, so the breath out is cut short.
items.why: A strong answer says that the voice and the breathing share the same air. It also says that exercise makes the body need fresh air sooner.

items.p: Draw the throat dividing into the windpipe and the food pipe. Show the epiglottis.
items.a: One passage behind the mouth divides into two tubes. The windpipe is in front, with the voice box at its top. The food pipe is behind. A flap, the epiglottis, sits above the opening of the windpipe.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one shared passage and two tubes below. The flap sits over the windpipe, and the food pipe stays open.
items.art: A blank side-view outline of a head and neck.

items.p: Which organ is the most important?

views.says: The heart. If the pump stops, nothing reaches any other organ.
The brain. The brainstem runs the breathing and the heartbeat.
None of them. When the kidneys fail, the heart and the brain soon fail too.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you know about the systems. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. For example, the heart cannot work without oxygen from the lungs and sugar from the gut and the liver.
items.why: Each view has something right. A strong answer follows at least one handover from one organ to another to make its point.

items.p: Why does your breathing stop for about a second when you swallow?
items.why: The voice box lifts and the epiglottis folds over the windpipe, so food cannot enter it. No air can pass until the swallow ends.

items.p: In hard exercise, which organs get less blood than at rest?
items.why: In the Hundred Beans, the gut and liver fall from 6 beans to 2. The kidneys fall from 5 to 2. Muscles, heart muscle and skin all get more.

items.p: Six hours after a meal, where does most of the sugar in your blood come from?
items.why: The liver turns its stored glycogen back into sugar and releases it. The lungs, bones and bladder do not store sugar.

items.p: Which organ makes urea, and which organ removes it from the blood?
opts: The liver makes it, the kidneys remove it
The kidneys make it, the liver removes it
The lungs make it, the skin removes it
The stomach makes it, the bladder removes it
items.why: The liver makes urea from used protein. The blood carries urea to the kidneys, which pass it out in urine.

items.p: A muscle can push a bone as well as pull it.
items.why: False. A muscle can only shorten, so it can only pull. That is why muscles work in pairs, one to bend a joint and one to straighten it.

items.p: A hormone reaches its target faster than a nerve signal does.
items.why: False. A nerve signal arrives in a fraction of a second. A hormone travels in the blood and takes seconds, minutes or hours.

items.p: Sort these organs. Does each one work in one system, or in two?
items.why: The pancreas digests and makes hormones. The throat carries air and food. The thigh bone holds you up and makes blood cells.

items.p: Three of these are parts of the brain. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A bronchus is an air tube leading into a lung. The other three are the main parts of the brain.

items.p: The kidneys get 5 beans of blood a minute. One bean is 200 millilitres. How many millilitres is that?
items.why: 5 beans of 200 millilitres each is 5 times 200, which is 1,000 millilitres. That is 1 litre every minute.

items.p: Blood returns from the body to the heart. Put its next stops in order.
items.why: Blood enters the right atrium and passes to the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs. It returns to the left atrium and then the left ventricle.

items.p: Running straight after a big lunch makes the stomach feel heavy. Use the Hundred Beans to explain why.
items.a: In hard exercise most of the blood goes to the muscles. The gut gets less than half of what it had at rest. So digestion slows, and the food stays in the stomach for longer.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers: the gut and liver fall from 6 beans to 2 while the muscles rise from 5 to 80.

items.p: On the Handover Map, cover the liver. Between meals, what would the leg muscles run short of, and why?
items.a: The muscles would run short of sugar. Between meals the small intestine has no more sugar to pass on. So the blood depends on the sugar that the liver releases from its glycogen.
items.why: A strong answer follows the arrows: liver to blood, blood to muscles. It names sugar as the thing handed over.

items.p: Humans use one throat for air and for food. Give one cost of this and one gain.
items.a: Cost: food can go down the windpipe and make us choke, so breathing must stop at every swallow. Gain: we can breathe through the mouth when the nose is blocked. We also shape breathed-out air into speech with the mouth.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real cost and a real gain. It does not call the shared throat simply good or simply bad.

items.p: Are the organ systems real divisions of the body, or lists made by people?

views.says: They are real. The organs of one system are joined by their own tubes and grow together before birth.
They are lists made by people. The throat, the pancreas and the bones each sit on two lists.
The lists are useful either way. I need them to find out what has gone wrong.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another view has right.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For example, in the card game Which System?, 10 of 24 organs belonged on two mats, which supports the philosopher. The joined tubes of the gut support the anatomist.
items.why: This is a real disagreement with no single winner. A strong answer uses a named organ as evidence and gives the other side a fair point.

items.p: Label the three main parts of the brain on this side view. Write one job beside each.
a: The cerebrum is the large top part. It does thinking, memory, speech and chosen movement.
The cerebellum is the small part at the lower back. It keeps your balance and makes movement smooth.
The brainstem is the stalk at the base. It runs breathing, heartbeat and swallowing.
items.why: The cerebrum is by far the largest part. The cerebellum sits under it at the back, and the brainstem leads down to the spinal cord.
items.art: A side view of a brain with three blank label lines.

items.p: A liver is washed until no sugar comes out. The next day it holds sugar again. What does this show?
opts: Sugar came in from the air
The liver makes bile from sugar
items.why: No food could reach the washed liver, so the new sugar must have come from a store inside it. That store is glycogen.

items.p: A child moves 24 beans alone, 17 while counting backwards and 23 while singing. What is the best conclusion?
opts: Two jobs that need attention slow each other
The hands were tired by the second round
items.why: Counting backwards cost 7 beans and singing cost only 1. Tired hands would have slowed the singing round as well.

items.p: An insect's blood carries almost no oxygen. How do the insect's cells get oxygen?
opts: Air tubes reach every part of the body
The insect does not need oxygen
items.why: Fine air tubes run from holes along the insect's sides to every part of the body. So in an insect, breathing does not depend on blood.

items.p: When a person's kidneys stop working, why does the heart come under strain?
opts: Spare water and salt stay in the blood
The heart has to make the urine
items.why: The kidneys let out spare water and salt. If they stop, the amount of blood grows and the heart must pump harder. The kidneys never pumped the blood.

items.p: Scientists agree that the human body has exactly 78 organs.
items.why: False. No group of scientists has agreed on a list. The number depends on what you count as one organ.

items.p: The urge to breathe comes mainly from carbon dioxide building up in the blood.
items.why: True. The brainstem measures carbon dioxide. When the level rises, it makes you breathe sooner and deeper.

items.p: Match each organ to its second, less famous job.
pairs: Sends a hormone to bone marrow
items.why: Each of these organs is known for one job and also does another. That is why each sits on two lists of systems.

items.p: A one-breath count lasts 19 seconds at rest and 6 seconds after step-ups. How many seconds shorter is that?
items.why: 19 take away 6 is 13. The count after exercise is 13 seconds shorter, less than a third of the resting time.

items.p: The flap that covers the windpipe during a swallow is called the ____.
items.why: The epiglottis sits behind the tongue. It folds down over the windpipe as the voice box lifts.

items.p: Many people think the brain gives all the orders. Give two pieces of evidence that other organs send messages too.
items.a: The heart makes a hormone that tells the kidneys to let out salt and water. Body fat makes leptin, which tells the brain how much fat is stored. The stomach and intestines make hormones about hunger.
items.why: A strong answer names two organs and says what each message does. It does not just say 'organs talk to each other'.

items.p: Plan a fair test of this question: does talking loudly use up a breath faster than talking softly?
items.a: Count aloud on one full breath, sitting at rest, once softly and once loudly. Time each count in seconds. Keep the person, the speed of counting and the rest between tries the same. Do three tries of each and compare the averages.
items.why: A strong plan changes only the loudness, measures seconds, keeps everything else the same and repeats each try.

items.p: After most swallows, the first breath is out, not in. Suggest why this could be safer for the lungs.
items.a: A breath out blows any drops left near the opening away from the windpipe. A breath in could pull them down into the lungs.
items.why: A strong answer links the direction of the air to where leftover drops would go.

items.p: A hospital machine can do the work of failed kidneys. What two things must the machine do to the blood?
items.a: It must take urea and other wastes out of the blood. It must also remove spare water and salt, and leave in the right amount of each.
items.why: A strong answer gives both jobs of the kidneys: removing wastes, and keeping water and salt at the right level.

items.p: How many organs does a body have?

views.says: Count every separate part. Each of the 206 bones is an organ, so there are hundreds.
Count by job. The whole skeleton is one organ, so there are fewer than a hundred.
It depends on the rule you choose. So I would rather ask what each part does.

items.ask: Which way of counting would you choose? Give a reason. Then say what your way of counting leaves unclear.
items.a: Any choice with a reason, and one honest weakness. Counting each bone gives a huge number and treats a toe bone like a liver. Counting by job makes it hard to place an organ with two jobs.
items.why: There is no agreed answer. A strong answer sees that the number depends on the definition of an organ.

items.p: Sketch a line graph of one-breath counting time: at rest, straight after exercise, and 1, 2 and 3 minutes later.
items.a: The line starts high at rest and drops to its lowest point straight after exercise. It climbs back towards the resting level over the next 3 minutes. The climb is steepest in the first minute.
items.why: A strong sketch shows the sharp drop and the gradual recovery, and does not rise above the resting level.
items.art: Blank graph axes, with 'When you counted' along the bottom and 'Seconds on one breath' up the side.

opts: A group of organs sharing one big job
The largest organ in the body
A group of cells of one kind
quiz.why: Organs that work together on one big job, such as digesting food, form an organ system. A group of cells of one kind is a tissue.

quiz.p: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood out to the whole body?
quiz.why: The left ventricle has the thickest wall, because it pumps blood all round the body. The right ventricle pumps only to the lungs.

quiz.p: Where does oxygen pass from the air into the blood?
quiz.why: The alveoli are tiny air bags wrapped in capillaries. The windpipe and throat only carry the air.

quiz.p: Which part of the brain runs your breathing and heartbeat?
quiz.why: The brainstem keeps breathing and heartbeat going without your thinking, even in sleep. The cerebrum does the thinking.

quiz.p: Which of these is an involuntary muscle?
opts: The muscle of the stomach wall
quiz.why: The stomach wall churns food without your choosing. You move the biceps, the tongue and the calf when you decide to.

quiz.p: In which organ does a baby grow before birth?
quiz.why: The uterus, or womb, is a bag of muscle where the baby grows for about nine months. The ovary only releases the egg.

quiz.p: Which organ works for both the digestive system and the hormone system?
quiz.why: The pancreas makes digestive juice and also the hormones insulin and glucagon. The other three each work in one system.

quiz.p: Why is a one-breath count shorter straight after exercise?
opts: The body must breathe in fresh air sooner
quiz.why: Working muscles add carbon dioxide to the blood, so the brainstem forces the next breath sooner. The lungs stay the same size.

quiz.p: In hard exercise, where does most of the blood go?
quiz.why: About four fifths of the blood goes to the working muscles. The gut and the kidneys get less, and the brain gets about the same as at rest.

quiz.p: Food and air take completely separate paths from the face down into the body.
quiz.why: False. Both pass through the throat. The paths divide lower down, into the windpipe and the food pipe.

quiz.p: Three resting counts were 18, 20 and 19 seconds. What is the average?
quiz.why: 18 + 20 + 19 = 57, and 57 ÷ 3 = 19. Choosing 57 means adding without dividing by the number of tries.

quiz.p: Which organ adds stored sugar to the blood between meals?
quiz.why: The liver stores sugar as glycogen and releases it when the blood needs more. The stomach only holds food that has just been eaten.

applications: Surgeons can move a healthy kidney from one person into another. The first lasting kidney transplant was done in Boston in 1954, between identical twin brothers. Surgeons in many Indian cities now transplant kidneys, livers and hearts.
A living person can give away part of their liver. The part that is left and the part that was given both grow. Each reaches nearly full size within a few months.
A dialysis machine does the work of failed kidneys. The Dutch doctor Willem Kolff built the first working one in the 1940s. It takes urea, spare water and spare salt out of the blood.
A small clip on a fingertip, called a pulse oximeter, measures how much oxygen the blood is carrying. Many families first saw one during the covid years.
Athletes use the 'talk test'. If you can still speak in full sentences while you run, the effort is moderate. If you can manage only a word or two, it is hard.

Singers and players of the nadaswaram, the flute and the shehnai train their breathing. They breathe in quickly and let the air out slowly. They are managing the one stream of air that breath and sound share.
People are taught not to talk or laugh with food in the mouth. Talking opens the windpipe, and food can then enter it.

open_questions.q: How many organs does the human body have?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have no agreed rule for what counts as one organ. In 2016 a surgeon argued that the mesentery, the sheet that holds the intestines, is an organ. Others still disagree.

open_questions.q: Does bone send a hormone that changes how people handle sugar?
open_questions.why_open: One team found this in mice in 2007. In 2020 two other teams could not find it. Nobody has shown it clearly in people.

open_questions.q: How does a liver know when to stop growing back?
open_questions.why_open: After part of a liver is removed, the rest grows until it is about the right size for the body. Then it stops. The signals that tell it to stop are only partly known.

open_questions.q: Can an organ from a pig work in a person for many years?
open_questions.why_open: In 2022 surgeons in the United States gave a man a pig's heart. The pig's genes had been changed to suit a human body. He lived for about two months. Later tries have lasted longer, but nobody yet knows the limit.

open_questions.q: Why can the brain not do two hard jobs at once without slowing down?
open_questions.why_open: The slowing is easy to measure, as in Beans and Threes. Scientists still argue about what exactly is in short supply.

maths.problem: In the One Breath Count, three counts at rest lasted 18, 20 and 19 seconds. What is the average?
maths.explain: Add the three tries: 18 + 20 + 19 = 57. Divide by the number of tries: 57 ÷ 3 = 19. So the average is 19 seconds.
maths.context: In the One Breath Count you time how long you can count aloud on one breath. You do it at rest and after one minute of step-ups. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Each try comes out a little different. The average of three tries is a fairer number to compare the exercise results with.

maths.problem: In the One Breath Count, the resting average was 19 seconds. Straight after step-ups the count lasted 6 seconds. About what fraction of the resting time is that?
maths.explain: 3 times 6 is 18, which is close to 19. So 6 seconds is about one third of 19 seconds.
maths.context: In the One Breath Count you time how long you can count aloud on one breath. You do it at rest and after one minute of step-ups. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'about a third' shows how big the drop was. '13 seconds less' would mean something different for a person whose resting time was 40 seconds.

maths.problem: After step-ups, the count was 6 seconds straight away. At 1, 2 and 3 minutes it was 11, 15 and 18 seconds. The resting average was 19. What do you expect at 4 minutes? Explain.
maths.answer: About 19 seconds, and no more than that.
maths.explain: The gains are 5, then 4, then 3 seconds, so they are getting smaller. The next gain would be about 2, which gives 20. But the count is returning to the resting level of 19, so it should level off there.
maths.context: In the One Breath Count you time how long you can count aloud on one breath. You do it at rest and after one minute of step-ups. These are made-up results.

maths.why_maths: A pattern in the numbers lets you predict the next one. Knowing the science tells you where the pattern must stop.

maths.problem: In the Hundred Beans, the kidneys get 5 of the 25 beans at rest. What fraction of the blood is that? How many litres a minute is it, if one bean is 200 millilitres?
maths.answer: One fifth of the blood, which is 1 litre a minute.
maths.explain: 5 out of 25 is the same as 1 out of 5. 5 beans of 200 millilitres make 1,000 millilitres, which is 1 litre.
maths.context: In the Hundred Beans, each bean stands for 200 millilitres of blood pumped in a minute. You share the beans among the organs, at rest and in hard exercise.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how large a share two small organs take. It explains why kidney trouble affects the whole body.

maths.problem: In the Hundred Beans, the brain gets 4 beans out of 25 at rest. In hard exercise the brain gets 4 beans out of 100. Did the brain get less blood in exercise? Explain.
maths.answer: No. The brain got the same amount, 800 millilitres a minute.
maths.explain: 4 beans is 4 times 200, which is 800 millilitres, in both rounds. The share fell from 16 in every 100 to 4 in every 100. That happened because the total grew four times, not because the brain lost any blood.
maths.context: In the Hundred Beans, each bean stands for 200 millilitres of blood pumped in a minute. You share the beans among the organs, at rest and in hard exercise.
maths.why_maths: A share and an amount are different things. Looking only at the share would wrongly suggest that the brain is starved in exercise.

maths.problem: In the Hundred Beans, the muscles get 5 beans at rest and 80 in hard exercise. The gut and liver get 6 at rest and 2 in exercise. How many times as much do the muscles get? What fraction of its resting supply does the gut keep?
maths.answer: The muscles get 16 times as much. The gut and liver keep one third.
maths.explain: 80 ÷ 5 = 16. For the gut and liver, 2 out of 6 is the same as 1 out of 3.
maths.context: In the Hundred Beans, each bean stands for 200 millilitres of blood pumped in a minute. You share the beans among the organs, at rest and in hard exercise.
maths.why_maths: Comparing by 'times as much' shows how strongly the body shifts its blood from digesting to moving.

maths.problem: In Your Largest Organ, a traced hand covers 96 squares of 1 square centimetre. One hand is about one hundredth of the skin. What is the area of the skin? Is it more or less than 1 square metre?
maths.answer: About 9,600 square centimetres, a little less than 1 square metre.
maths.explain: 96 × 100 = 9,600 square centimetres. One square metre is 100 centimetres by 100 centimetres, which is 10,000 square centimetres. 9,600 is 400 less than that.
maths.context: In Your Largest Organ you trace your hand on squared paper and count the squares. Then you use the rule that one hand covers about one hundredth of your skin.
maths.why_maths: Nobody can lay their skin flat to measure it. Multiplying one small area that you can measure gives an estimate of the whole.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that an organ can have more than one job? This card tells the true story of the liver and sugar.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1840s, most scientists held two ideas. The first was that each organ had one job, and the liver's job was to make bile. The second was that only plants could make sugar, and animals could only use it up. In 1848 the French scientist Claude Bernard fed dogs on meat alone, with no sugar or starch. He still found sugar in the blood leaving their livers. Was the sugar left over from older meals? In 1855 he washed water through the vessels of a liver until no more sugar came out. He left the liver until the next day. By then it was full of sugar again. The liver was making sugar from a store of its own. In 1857 he separated that store in pure form and named it glycogen. So the liver had at least two jobs, and through the blood it fed every other organ. Bernard tested living dogs, and many people thought this cruel. His wife, Fanny Martin, opposed his experiments on animals.
how_we_found_out.who: Claude Bernard, a French scientist, and his wife Fanny Martin, who opposed his tests on animals
how_we_found_out.when: 1848 (sugar found in blood leaving the liver), 1855 (the washed liver) and 1857 (glycogen)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That each organ has one job, and that animals cannot make sugar. Bernard showed that a liver washed clean of sugar makes sugar again, so the liver does more than make bile.
how_we_found_out.art: A nineteenth-century laboratory bench with a glass dish holding a liver, a jug of water and a row of test tubes, and a man in a dark apron writing in a notebook.

roots.context: In this unit you learned the organ systems, and you found organs that work in two systems. Here we ask what those shared parts tell us about a body.

deep_truth.truth: In the One Breath Count, you could count for far less time straight after the step-ups. Your voice and your breathing use the same stream of air, so your voice had to wait. Your throat is shared too, by air and by food. So one body part can work in two systems, and the two must take turns.
deep_truth.habit: We learn the organ systems as separate lists, as if each organ belonged to one list only. People made the lists, to make the body easier to study. The body uses one throat for air and food, and one stream of air for breathing and speaking.
deep_truth.evidence: In the One Breath Count, the counting time falls from about 20 seconds at rest to about 6 seconds straight after step-ups. It returns within about 3 minutes. In the Swallow Pause, breathing stops at every swallow. In the card game Which System?, 10 of the 24 organ cards belong on two mats.

three.who_am_i: You speak with your breath, and you breathe through the passage you eat with. Talking, eating and breathing are done by one body, using the same few parts in turn.
three.what_is_life: A living body does many jobs with only a few parts. So the parts must share and take turns every second. Most of this happens without you deciding anything.
three.what_is_this_world: A whale, a grasshopper and a child all need food and oxygen, and each body is arranged differently. The names of the systems come from the people who study bodies.

roots.thread: You began as one cell. That cell divided, and its daughter cells became bone, muscle, nerve, blood and gut. So all your organs are the descendants of one cell, doing different work. They never became fully separate. They share one supply of blood, one throat and one stream of air. When we name nine systems, we are describing one body, and each system is a different way of looking at it.

teachings.teaching: The text describes a person as five bodies, one inside the other: a body made of food, then bodies of breath, of mind, of understanding and of joy. Each one has the shape of a person and fills the one before.
teachings.link: In the Layer Book you draw one body on several see-through pages, one page for each group of systems. Every page fills the same outline. The Upanishad uses its layers to ask what the self is, which science does not test. What the two share is the idea that one body can be described fully in more than one way.

science.text: Every organ in your body grew from one fertilised egg cell.
Many organs do work for two or more organ systems, and many organs make hormones that act on other organs.
Are the organ systems real divisions in the body, or useful ways of describing one body? Anatomists and philosophers still argue about this.

other_view.view: The organ systems are real divisions. The organs of one system are joined by their own tubes, grow together before birth and often fall ill together. A kidney doctor must know the excretory system as one thing. Shared parts such as the throat are the exceptions. They do not show that the divisions were only made by people.

practice.title: Speak on the breath
practice.say: Sit comfortably. Breathe in, and as you breathe out, say your own name slowly. Notice that the sound ends when the air ends. Now breathe in again, and then swallow. Notice that your breathing waited for the swallow. Breathe quietly five times, and feel one throat do each job in turn.
practice.kid: Sit still. Breathe in. Say your name slowly as you breathe out. The sound ends when the air ends. Now swallow. Your breath waits. Breathe quietly five times.

ask: In the One Breath Count, your voice had to wait for your breathing. Who decided which one went first?
The throat is on two lists of systems. If you made your own list of the body's systems, how would you divide the body?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was reasoned through step by step. Each was pictured as a parent and child would do it in a city flat. None of them has been tried at home yet, so treat the expected results as likely, not certain. One Breath Count (core) needs a phone stopwatch, a clock and a low step, or jogging on the spot. A child of ten usually counts for 12 to 25 seconds at rest. Straight after a minute of step-ups the count is usually 4 to 8 seconds. It is nearly back after 3 minutes. Counts depend on how loudly and how fast the child counts, so keep both the same. The whole test takes about 40 minutes, with two runs and a 5-minute rest. The Swallow Pause (core) needs only water and a wet finger. The pause in breathing is easy to feel. Whether the next breath is out or in is harder to judge, and the cold spoon helps. Studies of grown-ups find that the first breath after a swallow is usually out, and children vary more. Beans and Threes needs 40 large beans and two bowls. A few children who are very quick at mental sums show little slowing. For them, count backwards in sevens. The Hundred Beans (core) needs 100 beans and seven bowls or paper labels. Its figures are rounded textbook values for a grown-up, not measurements of a child. Your Largest Organ uses the doctors' rule that one hand is about one hundredth of the skin. The rule is rough, and it gives a slightly low answer for grown-ups. Ruling the squares takes about 5 minutes. The Layer Book needs five see-through sheets. Thin white paper held against a window works if there is no tracing paper. The Throat Switch needs cardboard, tape and thread, and a grown-up to cut. The thread design works on the first or second try. The design with no thread is hard, and that difficulty is part of the challenge. Which System? has 24 cards, 10 of them with two systems, so the best score alone is 34. Chain It can be played alone by scoring against the backs of the cards. Nothing needs a garden or an animal. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026 against published sources: the cell count (about 30 trillion), the kidney filtering figure, the dates, names and papers in the stories, the transplant and dialysis facts, and the museum links. Softened: the red blood cell rate (now 'millions a second'), the length of the small intestine, the swallow breathing pattern, and the share of blood to the muscles in hard exercise. The Upanishad passage and the line from Marcus Aurelius are given as paraphrases. The three videos have no address yet.
